subsubtopic: DATE OF NEXT ELECTION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Since the Prime Minister has let election speculation get out of control over the last week, and his continued indecision and vacillation on the date of an election does not help our dollar or the unemployed, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):
That this House direct the Prime Minister to follow an old maritime custom and fish or cut bait, rather than continue his ego cat-and-mouse games with the body politic at the expense of the Canadian public.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Can he inform the House if VIA Rail, the government agency taking over rail

April 24, 1978
Oral Questions
passenger services, has under a proposed summer schedule change eliminated direct passenger service from eastern to western Canada which would mean a variety of inconvenient routes? For example, a passenger going from Ottawa to Banff will travel to North Bay, then to Sudbury by bus, where there will be a 12-hour wait for the train going farther west.
Will the schedule be implemented? If so, how does the minister justify the inconvenience and confusion which will be caused not only to Via Rail in terms of promotional work but also to the travelling public?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposed routes for VIA Rail are a matter of record. It is possible to go from eastern Canada to western Canada all the way through to Vancouver on a direct CN route or a direct CP route. Obviously, if one wants to make a change from the originating CN trackage to a Canadian Pacific destination, certain changes and waits are required. But that is true at the present time and is almost inevitable under any system.
What is intended in the VIA schedule is that a train going from the east through Montreal and Ottawa and then through the northern route across Canada to Winnipeg meets another eastern train from Toronto through Sudbury to Winnipeg and then, of course, from Winnipeg to Vancouver, each following respective CN-CP rail. Clearly, you cannot go from anywhere to everywhere in a direct way, and I should have thought that would be beyond what the hon. member would really demand.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Mr. D. Lewis, of VIA Rail, has confirmed that if the temporary summer schedule-which is what we are talking about-is okayed by the Canadian Transport Commission, there will be no direct routes to southern Alberta and some vacation areas in western Canada.
Would the government consider maintaining existing CN and CP services for the summer months, so there will be direct train service from one part of the country to another and not this confusion, and so VIA Rail will not get off to what appears to be a very bad start in the mind of the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret very much the expressions of concern, even by those who are supporters of VIA Rail, about the schedule. It is impossible to do everything which everyone might like in an ideal way, but this may save the taxpayers $30 million to $40 million and that is important. There is, of course, a very good eastern Canadian connection through to Banff. That is essentially a Canadian Pacific route.
Those who originate on a northern or CN route clearly have to change somewhere. It is possible to change at the Sudbury-Capreol area. It is true that would involve a bus connection. It is possible to change at Winnipeg, where there would be no bus connection because both trains arrive at Winnipeg. So it is possible to go from the northern route through to the southern routes. However, if one is moving from what has been a CN route to a CP route, one must change trains: a change is necessary. It is not possible to have a connection between every point in Canada to every other point without a change. As a

result of these changes we have better service at far less cost to the public. Both considerations, in my view, are very important.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the minister in the long term. But certainly in the short term, for the peak period this summer when people do most travelling, the proposed change of schedule will cause a great deal of confusion. It will cause chaos and VIA Rail will get off to a bad start, which I do not think anyone in this House of Commons wants to see. I would ask the minister one final supplementary question. In VIA's future plans is there talk of any change which would eventually eliminate the Vancouver-Jasper-Edmonton-Win-nipeg run which, of course, would be totally unacceptable to people in western Canada and to most Canadians?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this point there is no consideration of elimination of any runs. The Canadian Transport Commission produced its final plan, and that is the basic document with which VIA Rail is working. Of course, we all hope that VIA's management will come up with better ways of offering service to people who want to travel and will make proposals for schedule changes before the Canadian Transport Commission.
The immediate future, as fast as VIA can arrange it, will be to bring the trains from Toronto and Montreal together at one point in the Sudbury-North Bay area. Any problem which may arise in the first year of scheduling will therefore disappear. The very enthusiastic and energetic management of VIA and this whole new spirit of trying to make rail passenger service operate well again in Canada should be given a chance. We should avoid narrow, carping criticisms from day to day about some of the difficulties which are bound to occur.

Mr. Speaker, I would like a little clarification from the minister about VIA Rail. I think we all want to see it get off to a good start. My question concerns the fare structure, which I understand differs on CP and CN routes: one could wind up paying a substantially different price going from Montreal to Vancouver, for basically the same distance and the same service. Is this correct? If so, how long will it stay in place?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the rail structures we have been familiar with have been very different from CP to CN and even different in CN on different routes and on different days of the week. What VIA is now proposing, if it can get the necessary agreement and consent from the railways and the Canadian Transport Commission, is one uniform fare schedule in relation to movement across the country, regardless of the line of track on which the movement is made.
VIA is also attempting to bring about a fare schedule which is sensible from the point of view of the distance covered.
April 24, 1978

There is relativity with respect to rates between cities of equal distance apart and fares elsewhere in Canada. This is VIA's objective, and they are hoping to be able to move forward with that kind of rate schedule for June 1.

Mr. Speaker, can the minister give some assurance that a uniform rail fare structure will be in place by approximately June 1 ? Without this, VIA will be held responsible by passengers who are travelling the same distance and paying substantially different rates. Is this not likely to give VIA a black eye? One might ask why VIA took the service over before it was able to put a uniform rate schedule in place. Can the minister give assurance that this great possibility for misunderstanding and bad public relations will, in fact, be removed by roughly June 1 ?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is the objective. If VIA indeed takes over the service and is able to accomplish the changes required by June 1, that will be the case. If there are difficulties and we have rates which reflect different prices for the same distance in different parts of Canada, that will be a continuation of the existing situation and should in no way be laid at VIA's door by anyone.

May I, therefore, lay something at the door of the government? Advertising by the Canadian government office of tourism advertises VIA Rail vacations at a reasonable price, comfortable and different. They seem to be quite different today. Can the minister explain why the government is advertising in this way, putting VIA on the spot when he is in no position to give any assurance that this will in fact take place at any time on which he can put a firm date?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, VIA is already marketing the service and, therefore, in that sense will be associated with what is offered. I would like the hon. member to join in explaining that if there are any difficulties in moving toward a uniform, similar rate across the country it will not be VIA's responsibility but the inability to get, by that time, the necessary agreement from the railways. All that will remain is what has been in place for the past 10 or 15 years. I hope the hon. member will join me in hoping that the railways will co-operate in the ways required so that VIA Rail will be in a position to put a uniform, improved schedule in place, by June 1.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. Last year the Canadian Development Corporation acquired some $45 million worth of gas-producing property in Louisiana. Given the fact that we have over one million unemployed in our country, and the stated objective of CDC, according to the act, is to "assist in the creation or development of businesses, resources, properties
Oral Questions
and industries of Canada", does the government approve of CDC investment in the United States such as the purchase made in Louisiana?
Mr. Speaker, I will look into the question and report to the hon. member.

In light of the fact the Canadian government controls some two-thirds of CDC voting stock and has two deputy ministers, including the minister's deputy, sitting on the board of directors, will the minister advise whether it is the intention of the government to direct the CDC to expand and invest in Canada rather than in other countries such as the United States?

Mr. Speaker, it is possible that in some circumstances they have decided, in the best interests of the corporation and its long-term goals, to invest in foreign ventures; but basically CDC is investing in Canada.

Quite apart from what the CDC is doing, there has been a dramatic increase of investment by Canadian companies and private citizens in other countries, primarily the United States. Is the minister concerned about this move in Canada regarding the flow of capital outside our country? If the Canadian government is concerned, is it contemplating any action to stop this trend?

Mr. Speaker, there is a free flow of capital between Canada and the United States. We are not planning to impose any foreign exchange control. It is basically a matter of the investment policies of the individual. There are some distorted factors in those figures. In some cases money went to the United States, but it has been a case of Canadians buying Americans' interests in Canada. It seemed as though it was investment in the United States, but it was just buying back Canadian interests.

subtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF TARIFF CUTS-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT
PROPOSED EXTENSION OF TARIFF CUTS-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. It concerns the minister's decision to extend permanently the 1973 tariff cuts which were due to expire on June 30 this year. Will the minister tell the House, in light of the promise made by his predecessor, John Turner, to monitor the impact of the cuts, what the precise effects of the tariff reductions were in terms of jobs; and, further, will he now table whatever reports have been made of the impact of the tariff reductions?

subtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF TARIFF CUTS-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know if there is any monitoring of the precise tariff cuts but I will inquire. If we have that information, I will gladly report it to the hon. member.

speechtext:
It appears that the minister made the decision to renew the cuts on such items as drugs and pharmaceuticals, kitchen and dinnerware, furniture, house trailers, photographic equipment, all of which could be produced by Canadian

April 24, 1978
Oral Questions
industry, without having any real information on the effect of the cuts in the first place. Will the minister tell the House why he did not initiate a full-scale study of the impact of the cuts, especially in light of Mr. Turner's promise to this House?

subtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF TARIFF CUTS-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I said that I would inquire and report my findings to the hon. member. Of course, these tax cuts were made at that time to help reduce the cost of living in Canada.

speechtext: By unilaterally renewing the tariff reductions, the minister seems to have thrown away a good negotiating card. subtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION OF TARIFF CUTS-EFFECT ON EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I have extended the temporary cuts. We have not made them definitive.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. As it has been widely reported by the press and members of the Prime Minister's party that a decision to call a general election is being held up because of unsatisfactory poll results coming out of Toronto and southern Ontario, might I ask the Prime Minister whether he has now decided when he is going to call an election or whether he has chosen to continue to govern by Gallup poll?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State (Environment). Because of the continuing need for effective reforestation programming, and because of the need to upgrade certain species of trees in Canada in order to provide
April 24, 1978

for the future requirements of Canada's forest-based industries, is the government prepared to make a commitment that an adequate percentage of the dollars earned through our international sales of forest products will go toward reforestation and upgrading of our forests in various woodland areas of Canada? The upgrading of our forests would help make us more competitive.
Second, is the minister's department continuing to do research work to develop and produce particular disease-resistant types of trees in order to protect future forest resources from natural enemies such as Dutch elm disease, spruce budworm, and so forth?

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Forestry Service has a program under which it is developing better species and better productivity, more disease-resistant, more insect-resistant, and so on. Discussions are now going on with a number of provinces relative to reforestation. It is hoped that my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, will be able to reach agreement with a number of provinces to implement reforestation programs using Canada Works funds.
With regard to basing possible support for regeneration programs on the value and amount of forest products exported from Canada, I must advise the hon. member that the federal government has no such plans.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE TO RCA TO PREVENT LAY-OFFS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. We in eastern Ontario were very discouraged to learn that RCA has announced the closing of another plant in Ontario. Two years ago, 440 jobs were lost in Renfrew. RCA is going to put another 300 people out of work, allegedly because its plant is not competitive and needs to be automated.
Since the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is not here, I wonder if the Minister of Employment and Immigration can comment on the steps his department will take to try to find jobs for the 300 people who will be unemployed in an area which already has 12 per cent unemployment. Would the minister take up this matter with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and encourage him, through his department, to allow a grant to RCA in Smiths Falls, Ontario, so that the plant there can be automated, become competitive and keep people working?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Considering that mortgage prepayment penalties are a growing source of complaint for consumers, and the claim that federal law seems to be unclear whether after five years mortgage holders may give three months' notice of prepay-

ment and thereby avoid the assessment of prepayment charges, and in view of the fact that mortgage companies are inconsistent in their assessment of prepayment penalties to mortgage holders, assessing no charge to home owners with mortgages under 8 per cent but charging extra interest to others, could the minister inform this House what steps he is taking to clarify the principle of law contained in the Interest Act of Canada in order to protect consumers better?

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the borrowers and depositors protection legislation which was tabled by my predecessor in the last session of parliament would have repealed the Interest Act. It contained provisions to control conditions for mortgage prepayment in favour of the mortgagor. That bill died on the order paper at the end of the last session in September. Since that time, we have been consulting business and consumer interests in order to improve the bill. It is our hope to introduce an improved bill with mortgage prepayment provisions as soon as possible.
I think I should point out, however, that the hon. member for York-Simcoe said, on behalf of the Conservative party, that if we were to reintroduce that bill he would do everything possible to oppose it.
Shame.

DRILLING FOR OIL AND GAS WELLS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Last week the Canadian Petroleum Association released data indicating that oil and gas drilling activity in Canada's frontier lands under federal jurisdiction continued to decline in 1977, and that out of a total of 6,200 wells drilled in
Oral Questions
Canada only 28 were drilled on federal lands. This means, in percentage terms, that activity on federal lands is one-eighth of what it was in 1972, five years ago. Can the minister tell the House if this decreasing oil and gas drilling on federal lands is in keeping with federal government policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: DRILLING FOR OIL AND GAS WELLS ON CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is true that proportionately there has been less activity in the frontier regions than there has been in other parts of the country, particularly in Alberta and British Columbia. Order, please. That matter has now been reraised by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). It gives the Chair the always difficult decision of determining whether or not the remark made by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), having to do with the ethics or morals of the minister, has to be withdrawn in terms of parliamentary precedents. I must say that the matter is made a little simpler by a balancing event which took place at noon the following day when, during the course of an exchange between the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of Finance made a statement about which the hon. member for York-Simcoe complained in a similar way. That statement was, and I quote from page 4744 of Hansard:

Before we go too far in this matter, I do not believe that I, or the members of parliament who have had any experience in this House, or for that matter the members of the public, I am sure, are about to fall over in a faint at the sound of the words that were used in either of those occasions. But that is not the point.
The point is simply that in the conduct of our debate we are entitled and encouraged to say vigorous and strident things about the performance of people on opposite sides of the House and other parties. This is the way parliament should operate. However, in the course of doing so, whenever we cross the line and enter into personal reflections, instead of reflections on matters of policy or performance of the duty of hon. members or of a party, and things of that nature, we always get into an unfortunate incident, such as these instances that are before us at this time.
Frankly, I do not take as much umbrage at such instances as my predecessors have done. However, I wish to remind the House that what my predecessors were doing, and what I have to do, is not guard my own sensitivity to these kinds of remarks, but guard the sensitivity of the House of Commons now and for all time in the future.
We must adhere to a certain standard of language and a certain standard of conduct in the House, in order to maintain a proper standard of dignity in respect to the debates here.

Inevitably, every time we get away from the substance of debate and cross over into the area of personal reflection, on the one side or the other, we always run a very high risk of putting that whole sense of dignity and decorum in jeopardy.
I could quite easily come to the conclusion that neither of these exchanges was unparliamentary in nature and neither ought to be withdrawn. However, my inclination, rather than letting the matter extend any further, is to indicate if the one is, then so is the other, but the much safer course is to preserve for the future that level of decorum in this House and that we not cross over from the general area of discussion before the House into matters of personal reflections. In other words, in the circumstances in which the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton found himself, it was quite open to him to get up in his place, if he had the opportunity during the course of the debate, and say that he was very critical of the performance of the Minister of Transport and that he found that it, in fact, may have some other reflections, about which he could have asked the House to conclude. Similarly, the Minister of Finance on Friday could have stood up and said that "the hon. member for York-Simcoe has said this and, Mr. Speaker, here is the record, and I want members to judge."
Not that I want the House to judge whether it is ethical or moral, but on Thursday night the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton went one step further when he stood up and said the minister has the morals of an alley cat-and, similarly, on Friday when the Minister of Finance said that the hon. member can be dishonest in this way-instead of putting the facts before the House and asking the House to judge. MR. LAWRENCE-ROLE OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL REVENUE VIS-A-VIS HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege on a completely different matter which affects all members of this House. It is a basic tenet of the British parliamentary system that the ministry, collectively and individually, is responsible to the House of Commons. We are, hopefully, in an embarrassingly short period when the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Guay) does not sit in this chamber.
Last Thursday or Friday when I spoke to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) about this matter I understood from him, or perhaps I should say I misunderstood from him, that he was taking upon his shoulders the position of acting Minister of National Revenue, or at least would be responsible to this House for that department. Obviously I misunderstood what the minister said because today, when a question was directed to him relating to that department, he sat in his seat waiting for someone who is not a member of the ministry to answer the question.
I think this is a serious matter, Mr. Speaker. We should have someone responsible for each of the departments in this House. This is not to say there has to be a minister in this House for each of the departments, but there has to be a minister responsible in the House for each of the departments. There is a difference. That has certainly been the parliamentary tradition. If it is abridged, I suggest to you it destroys one of the basics of the British parliamentary procedure under which we operate and sometimes suffer. Nevertheless, it is there.
I think we should know-and I hope you do, sir-if there is a member of the ministry who is responsible in this House for the Department of National Revenue. I suggest to you, sir, if
April 24, 1978

you do not know the answer either, we should get that answer from you, sir, and you should use your office to get it from either the government House leader or Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), or whoever is in control of the government.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MR. LAWRENCE-ROLE OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL REVENUE VIS-A-VIS HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
With respect, Mr. Speaker, I suggest the hon. member may be confusing two issues. First, is there an acting minister? The answer is yes. By order in council we always establish not only one acting minister but two acting ministers in the event that a minister should be away and action has to be taken in his department or in the House on his behalf. There are two acting ministers. The list has been distributed, as is customary, not only to the opposition but has been made public in the Canada Gazette.
The second question is, who in the House of Commons answers questions? I think it has been clearly stated by you and your predecessor, sir, that parliamentary secretaries have, as one of their functions, to answer questions. We attempt to answer questions as best we can. It is easier when notice is given in advance. The questions are put for the purpose of seeking information and we attempt to co-operate and give that information when we are advised of questions. Who can best give this information? The practice, as long as I have been in the House, has been that when the parliamentary secretary is present, when he has been briefed, when he has the information or is able to vouch for its obtainment, he gives the answer. This does not mean there is not a minister or acting minister, but we seek to have the answer given by the person more likely to achieve the result wanted by the opposition. These matters are quite distinct. I submit to you that the government has been following well-established parliamentary practice.

subtopic: MR. LAWRENCE-ROLE OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL REVENUE VIS-A-VIS HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having been in this House somewhat longer than the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and having been here when the Parliamentary Secretaries Act was set up, may I suggest to him that it is quite well established a parliamentary secretary does not state policy on behalf of the ministry or the government. That is quite clearly understood. When an acting minister responds for the government, however, that can be a statement of policy and there is responsibility.
Most of the practice has been for a parliamentary secretary merely to say he will take a question as notice because he cannot speak on behalf of the government under these circumstances.
With the greatest deference I would suggest that the confusion is in the mind of the Prime Minister on this particular point. What my colleague, the hon. member for Northumber-land-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), is saying is that he wants to be able to question an acting minister who can speak for the government. That is the only clarification that is wanted.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. LAWRENCE-ROLE OF MINISTER OF NATIONAL REVENUE VIS-A-VIS HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
This matter has been contributed to many times in the past. The final conclusion has always been-and I will venture to say it would be no different under these circumstances-that the role of the parliamentary secretary in respect of endeavouring to take questions and deal with them
Fisheries and Forestry
on behalf of his or her minister in the House, relates to the general obligation of the government to give answers to questions and to give them in some sort of satisfactory way. That is not a procedural obligation, and it is not an obligation which can be enforced by the Chair in the first instance. Therefore, if any effort is made to give any kind of answer, the judgment of the quality of that contribution to the question period is one that must be made in other than procedural senses and is outside the authority of the Chair.
I have no authority to compel an answer and, therefore, no authority to decide whether a parliamentary secretary does or does not properly answer for a minister in this House. The House resumed from Friday, April 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Horner that Bill C-36, to amend the Export Development Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, on rising this afternoon I would like to know who on earth is responsible for this bill on the government side. As far as I can see, neither the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) nor his parliamentary secretary are here. His parliamentary secretary was here some time ago but he is not here at the present time. I think that this is just a further indication by the minister in question of the almost contempt in which he holds this House.
Order, please. The Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) on a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I am the Acting Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I am here to listen to the hon. member with rapt interest.
April 24, 1978
Wrap it up.

Mr. Speaker, this is a grave revelation considering the exchange that my colleague, the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), had with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) concerning the Acting Minister of National Revenue. The Prime Minister would not disclose who the acting minister was, and the questions were to be put to parliamentary secretaries. I am glad to see my hon. friend here in the capacity of Acting Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce so that there is somebody here; I now see the parliamentary secretary is back here too.
If there is to be an answer made, I trust it will be made by the minister in question. This hon. member here has not got, shall we say, the awkward position into which the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has put himself by some of his statements with regard to trying to get passage of this bill through the House rather expeditiously, on an earlier occasion. I am going after the reputation of that minister and his behaviour in this House, one side or the other. The two are not reconcilable. I want to place that straight on the record.
I know all about this bill. I saw the president of the Export Development Corporation at a meeting months ago. At that time he indicated that this would be the situation. We are fully aware of it. This is stupidity, and that is all I can call it, Mr. Speaker, sheer stupidity in handling government affairs with regard to this bill. This bill was preceded by Bill C-39 regarding debasement of gold coins in this country-terribly important, I am sure. All it wants to do is get the government off the hook for the snafu with regard to the Olympic gold coins and the difficulties they had with the House; another way to trying to bypass parliament.
This particular bill, Bill C-36, I agree is an important bill, far more important than a lot of the tripe put before us prior to this. Then the minister on Friday had the gall to say that he wanted the House to pass this bill quickly on second reading so that it could go to committee, be considered ahead of the estimates, and get passed ultimately under some sort of deadline. Overriding this whole situation is the cat and mouse game of the Prime Minister with regard to the election date. The minister says, "Well, you better pass my bill before I get it caught by the guillotine of the election." Now, is that the way to run a shop? I say no. It is just crass incompetence on the part of that minister. I do not care whether he says that he tried to consult somebody on this side to see whether he could get expeditious passage.
There is no way any minister, least of all the member from Crowfoot, is going to say that a bill requires expeditious passage. I have heard him, year in and year out, and I am not talking about caucus secrets or anything like that, standing in his place on this side, berating ministers for the speed with which they wanted legislation. As I have said, he thinks that he is now responsible, that he has become a statesman. It only indicates the two standards in thinking which that minister has. I am sure the people in his constituency will be fully aware of that. Certainly the people of Alberta will be more
Export Development Act
than fully aware of it because they will be hearing a great deal more about it too.
Something else happened which came to my attention over the weekend. We did a little bit of digging in another file. I have a letter before me from the Canadian Export Association. It is dated March 28, 1978, addressed to Robert Kaplan, M.P., chairman of the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs of this House. The letter is signed by our old friend, Tommy Burns. Mr. Burns was a former senior assistant deputy minister for the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. In his capacity now he is president of a lobby group, the Canadian Export Association. With all due respect to Mr. Burns, and I always got along well with Mr. Burns-I had a great deal of appreciation of his abilities as a senior public servant-I do find it objectionable that he should write to the chairman asking, and I quote:
... for your support for the expeditious passage of the bill regarding the Export Development Corporation recently introduced in the House of Commons.
He goes on to say:
Any inability of EDC to support the efforts of Canadian exports through long-term lending, insurance, or support for bid bonds and performance guarantees relating to export contracts, will have a very serious impact on Canadian [exports, with a consequent] effect on employment in Canada.
The concluding paragraph states:
If your Committee would want to have more detailed views from the Association, we would be very glad to provide [either in a written] brief or in an appearance at one of your hearings.
We certainly would on that point. What I object to is this orchestrated lobbying by a former insider of the department, as a matter of fact a senior officer of the department, to get this bill through, it coming through so late in the year.
I have a further letter dated March 20, signed by H. W. Godwin, the president of Seismic Service Supply (1958) Limited, Calgary. He is a director of EDC and planning to be a private Canadian businessman relying on the facilities of EDC in our export business from time to time. He states:
-I respectfully urge you to support this bill through the legislative process with every possible haste.
This is a personal letter addressed to me from a director of EDC. Is there some sort of a con game going on here? Why this pressure?
As I said before, I have fully discussed the performance, the problems, and the future of the Export Development Corporation with senior officials of that corporation, at the invitation of the president. I understand their situation. I may have some different views on what they offer.
Why do we get this sort of pressure on the side? Certainly Mr. MacDonald will have to explain why he gets the non-government directors of the Export Development Corporation to lobby individuals members about quick passage of this bill. If these men are experienced in the ways of government, the blessed bill should have been in the hopper a long time ago. It is not necessarily the fault of the EDC. They certainly made their requirements known to the government a long time ago.

If they did not, they should have. The matter of when they made their requirements known to the government will have to be cleared up.
We are in this bind today as a result of incompetence in the legislative process of this administration who have got their tails caught up in a snarl on every side. Frankly, this type of administrative snafu is one of the reasons why it is high time this government was sent packing. Why is it so late in the day? No matter how expeditiously this House deals with it, the Finance committee has a currency bill before it. If anybody reads what I had to say on Friday afternoon, they will see that the responsibility of the Finance committee is to deal with the estimates of this House. It must be remembered that the responsibility of parliament with regard to supply is the principal reason it is there. It is not there to pass amendments to bits and pieces of bills. That is a secondary purpose. It is the operations of government through the examination of the granting of supply that rate number one. This has been a standing principle ever since I have come to parliament.
There are some who might think that efficiency in government depends on the number of bills passed. All you have to do to pass bills is to sit here silent, get wide in the flank, and wider between the ears. Bills will pass, but they are not the measure of the efficiency of government or of the performance of this House.
I want to make something clear. The prime role of this chamber and the membership thereof, between the end of January and early February, when the estimates come down and are referred to the various standing committees, and May 31, is the detailed consideration of estimates. We need to have a block system. There are only so many sessions during which committees may sit, when House personnel are available, and the membership is available for those committees.
At the expense of the consideration of the estimates, there are some who insist that we consider a gaggle of bills in committee. This is particularly true of the finance committee by reason of its jurisdiction in dealing with all sorts of matters that have to do with economic affairs.
The finance committee necessarily attracts more bills to it year in and year out. A former chairman, the Minister of State (Multiculturalism) (Mr. Cafik), will be a real witness to that. In fact anyone who sat as chairman of that committee will readily agree. However, to expect them to pass between February 1 and May 31 is totally misreading the situation. There are ways of dealing with it, but not within the present framework that we have for a committee structure. No way!
Committees cannot sit from early morning until late at night every day. There are those, including departmental advisers, who, frankly, have to go back to the drawing board and learn all over again the workings of parliament. We can accomplish the business, provided it is properly organized and brought forward early enough. This bill has been in the contemplation of the Export Development Corporation for months and months. They can forecast their requirements. As a matter of fact, the bill goes far beyond their present requirements. It is not a question of giving them annual supply. It is a

total structure that will remove them from coming before the House for years, unless inflation keeps galloping at the present rate.
I do not disagree with the principle of giving them borrowing limits or ceilings with regard to the contingent liabilities to ensure their contracts so they do not have to come back to parliament every year. I agree with that. We agreed about that months ago.
Why is this bill now before us under the guillotine of a pending election? As a matter of fact, according to all the portents, parliament could have been dissolved on not one, but two occasions in the past fortnight. The hon. member from Bonaventure asked me-
-Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine!

-Iles-de-la-Madeleine-I am sorry, it used to be Bonaventure. The hon. member for Bonaventure-iles-de-la-Madeleine is asking me how we can possibly know this. Well, he reads newspapers as we do. He listens to the radio. He has his own colleagues who are saying the same thing. And some of his colleagues have told me that they hoped the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would put an end to this.
Newspapers cannot be trusted!

I agree. And he says now that newspapers cannot be trusted. Well, that is something else again. I wonder how many of his colleagues share his opinion that one should not believe everything one reads in the papers. You can always go and talk about this to newspapermen. Go and share your opinions with them.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude this part of my intervention by saying how surprised I am to see that a minister who deems this bill to be of such tremendous importance could not be present in the House and was satisfied with having his acting minister try and reply to our questions. I am well aware that the acting minister is not too well informed of what this bill is all about and therefore of what he should reply to the questions some of my colleagues and I are about to ask him.

I want to get back to some questions which I am sure the minister or his officials will have to answer in committee. I am referring to the financial statement for the year ended December 31, 1976. Unfortunately I do not have a statement for 1977, which would have been far better; we have not been able to put our hands on it though I trust such a document does exist, in which case I hope one of my hon. friends will make reference to it and to the newer figures it must contain. I should like to know why there was an increase between 1975 and 1976 of about 25 per cent in administrative expenditures
April 24, 1978

and whether this increase has been matched in the period 1977-78.
There are items in this financial statement, such as those relating to shareholders equity and the disposition of retained earnings, which will have changed so much in the past year that it would be less than useful to go into an examination of their significance or put questions with regard to them at this time. I realize that because this document is concerned with 1976 it would be unrealistic to deal with it now.
Certainly we want this bill to go to committee. We shall talk to representatives of the Export Association there and we may want to talk to some other people as well. I would suggest that in the interval the parliamentary secretary or the chairman of the finance committee, before deciding when any meetings should be held, should call a meeting of a steering committee to obtain the views of members as to the manner in which these matters could be dealt with best. Some serious meetings have been arranged with ministers to deal with estimates and these will more than occupy the attention of hon. members. Besides, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) gave notice this afternoon that he wants the bill dealing with customs tariff changes arising out of the recent budget considered in the House, and there is no way in which meetings of the finance committee could be scheduled at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the bill before us today, the bill introduced by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) on Friday. It is unfortunate that the minister is not present in the chamber today, but I see the acting minister is here in his place.
As we all know, the Export Development Corporation was established in 1969 to succeed the Export Credit Insurance Corporation which had been in operation since 1944. The EDC does a number of things which, I suppose, are necessary. Almost all the industrialized states around the world have export development corporations of one sort or another through which governments assist exporters, presumably because they realize they have to do so in order to maintain jobs at home. The interesting thing is that, despite the work of the Export Development Corporation here, we support our exports to a lesser degree than do most of our trading partners. These are the figures as supplied by Statistics Canada for 1976: Canada supports its exporters to the tune of about 5 per cent of the value of the exports. Figures for other countries are as follows: the United States, 8 per cent; West Germany, 10 per cent; France, 39 per cent; Great Britain, 45 per cent; Italy, 9 per cent; Japan, 49 per cent. Despite the operations of the EDC we are not promoting the export of our commodities, technology and so on, to the extent other countries do.
One 'can see, also, from the figures I have given, that the arguments raised in this House during the Alcan debate by my hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, my hon. friend from Sault Ste. Marie, and others, are indeed very credible. Japan supports its exports to a much greater degree than any other industrial country. This is one reason we have to be very concerned about the Alcan route, whether the
Export Development Act
pipeline is actually built with Canadian steel and whether it is our steel mills which will provide the pipe, supply the jobs, and so on. We have a great deal to fear from Japan because of the way in which the government of that country supports exports.
In any case, the EDC has been in operation since 1969, and its functions are really threefold. First, it offers insurance to the various companies which export goods around the world; second, it extends export loans; and third, it offers insurance for the foreign investments of firms operating in countries where the political climate may not be particularly stable. The corporation helps in many ways. In my own region of the prairies it has assisted in the export of grain and the other commodities we produce.
There are four matters of concern to me that I wish to place before the acting minister this afternoon. One of the concerns I have is the support given by the Export Development Corporation to Canadian companies which invest abroad.
We know, for example, that the federal government has supported the International Nickel Company for quite some time through various tax concessions and the like. Despite that, jobs have been lost at Sudbury and Thompson, Manitoba. The reason for that is the over-supply of nickel in the world. Despite the fact that there is an over-supply of nickel in the world, we find that the Export Development Corporation has been supporting Inco in its investments in Indonesia and Guatemala. Between 1973 and 1976 about $78 million went to Inco so that it could expand its facilities and plants in Indonesia and Guatemala. The Export Development Corporation is financed by taxpayers, and it is giving money to a Canadian corporation to expand in foreign countries and take jobs away from Canadian workers. This is a good example of the corporation's doing the exact opposite to what it was established for in the first place. It was established to create jobs, to build up our exports, and to make sure that we are more competitive in the world community.
When the acting minister responds, I hope he will deal seriously with this. It does not seem right that we should be giving money to Inco to go to places like Guatemala and Indonesia. We could say that those loans are one of the reasons why we have an over-supply of nickel in the world and one of the reasons, why Canadian workers here are losing their jobs. To me that does not seem right. It does not seem to be the type of priority the Export Development Corporation should adopt.
One of the reasons Inco goes to Guatemala and Indonesia is that there are very low wage rates in those countries. Inco can hire local workers for just a few dollars a day or a few cents an hour to work in its mines. That is why Inco wants to go to third world countries to develop. Inco wants to compete with other huge internationals around the world in order to make a buck. I do not blame Inco for that. Under our system the purpose of a large corporation is to make money, to exploit people, to exploit resources, to make a few bucks for its shareholders, and to make itself more powerful in the world

Export Development Act
community. Elowever, when a company receives all kinds of grants to develop industries here at home, it should not be allowed to invest in other countries and to use taxpayers' money in order to make its investments profitable for a few shareholders.
My second concern-and I would like the acting minister to respond, if he possibly can-is that it has been reported that a number of other companies will be receiving or are receiving money from the Export Development Corporation to expand in other countries around the world. The result of that will not just be larger companies but, more important, Canadian jobs will be lost.
The first example I want to use was raised in the question period today by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes). The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) was not aware of the details and agreed to take notice of the question on behalf of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The question dealt with a company called Co'steel International of Whitby, Ontario. As reported in August by the financial newspapers, this company received some $47 million toward a $94 million project to build a steel mini-mill in New Jersey. The company will receive, or has received, $47 million from the Export Development Corporation. This company was an adviser to the Cansteel consortium formed by the Nova Scotia government to revive the province's steel industry. It had to abandon plans to build a plant on Cape Breton Island last year when a government consultant said the world's steel market could not justify the construction of a new plant.
This is rather interesting. We find that the company cannot justify building a new plant on Cape Breton Island because of the world steel market's being soft, yet a Crown corporation financed by you, Mr. Speaker, me and everybody else in this country, gives some $47 million to a Canadian company to build a steel mill in the United States. I am sure the Americans do not need Canadian tax dollars to build a steel mill. The Americans have a competitive economy of their own, and I am sure that money could be better utilized in our own country to expand our steel industry in places like Cape Breton, Sault Ste. Marie, Hamilton or, indeed, in my own province of Saskatchewan.
The Ipsco steel plant in Regina or the Ipsco plant in Edmonton could be expanded. The Ipsco plant in Edmonton has been waiting for a long time for an announcement by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion of money so that it can expand its facilities. These companies want to expand their facilities because they want to be in a good position to compete for the tenders on the pipeline which is about to be built in this country to take American gas from Alaska to the main part of the United States.
This government is spending money to build a steel mill in New Jersey. I have a knowledge of that area, and I just do not think that makes any sense. There are one million people in this country who are unemployed, and it seems to me that all investment priorities should be channelled in a planned, coordinated and rational way toward resolving the big problem we have, unemployment. must be our priority, and if we channel all government programs into resolving that problem I am sure that with the resources, money, talent and skills we have in Canada we could, over the span of a few short years, put our people to work and build an even better country called Canada in which, we, our children, and our grandchildren, can live.

Mr. Speaker, in considering Bill C-36 I think we must look for a trick or two in it. It is not until you get through quite a few pages that you find what are the real implications of this bill. Let me refer to a summary I made showing the various clauses of the bill and the sections that are going to be changed, and the effect these various clauses have on the structure of the Export Development Corporation at the moment.
To start with, in clause 1, having to do with the capital of the EDC, we find the share capital is being changed from $400 million to $1,000 million, or $1 billion. Therefore, in general, the reference to dollar commitments or dollar exposure is on a ten times basis, so that instead of reading a figure of $10 billion later on, for instance, in clause 3, which amends Section 26 of the existing act, the reference should be, the contingent liability on corporate account is an exposure ten times the share capital of the corporation, and that translates into $10 billion, which is four times the present limit of $2.5 billion.
The same clause changes section 28 of the Act, that is, the $1 billion figure to $3.5 billion, an increase of 3.5 times, and in clause 4 we find that Section 30 is being changed. The guarantees on corporate account are increased from $4.25 billion to $10 billion. Clause 5 of the bill increases the guarantees on government account from $850 million to $2.5 billion. Altogether that means that the commitments the EDC will have under the new act will be precisely three times what they were. In other words, the total of share capital and commitments at the present moment is $9 billion. Under the new proposals the total will be three times that, or $27 billion.
I am suggesting that these really are quite important commitments we are dealing with during the debate on this bill, amounting to an increase of $18 billion. We should ask ourselves what it is exactly that we are financing with this Export Development Corporation. The government may tell us it is creating all kinds of jobs for Canadians and so on, but I think we have to look at what has happened.
We can see that the Canadian government has financed a pulp mill in Poland and steel mills in the United States, and reference has been made to those already. Where are the jobs
[Mr. Nystrom.l
for Canadians. That is what we want to see, as we have over one million unemployed now and we want those jobs for Canadians. The minister has told us that jobs will be given to Canadians through construction of this machinery. That is true, but this is a one-time sale, and I will come back to that in a moment.
The projection we would like to see is some kind of a national development corporation with funding which would not be restricted necessarily to export sales, but would in the long run improve Canadian job prospects.
If we take that kind of idea, recognizing that the development of export sales is one of our principal national objectives, but by no means the only one, in the hands of the Export Development Corporation the pursuit of export has too often been a single-minded undertaking, undertaken at all costs and at the expense of other more overriding domestic aims. In too many cases there has been a trade-off of our long term national objectives, such as permanent employment, for the short term benefits of a specific contract, such as those about which the minister told us.
I want to go into a little more detail about the two recent examples I referred to a moment ago. Recently the EDC committed $160 million to financing a pulp mill in Poland. There is no doubt that this low cost loan underwritten by the taxpayers of Canada enables Canadian firms to sell this equipment abroad. It is also quite clear that the Poles, whom everyone expects to be among our chief competitors in the European pulp and paper market, are really the beneficiaries of that deal. The Poles will get the new mill and the new permanent jobs. We in Canada will have to content ourselves with the fact that we helped to finance the creation of jobs in Poland, at the expense of jobs here at home, in order to gain one export contract.
I referred earlier to steel mills in the United States. The EDC agreed last summer to put up $47 million for a new steel mill in New Jersey. That brought to a total of $100 million the amount loaned by the EDC for steel mills in Minnesota, Texas, and New England. Once again with the steel mill a Canadian firm got the contract, so there was a short term benefit to Canada, but once again it was the Canadian interests that lost out in the long run. It is the Americans, not Canadians, who get the permanent jobs resulting from this contract, and these are the very steel plants in New Jersey which will eventually compete against our own Canadian steel manufacturers, to the detriment of Canadian jobs. We have already seen the government do an about face recently in respect of tariffs on imported steel. First it put a tariff on, and then it removed it temporarily as it affects British Columbia and some other marginal provinces.
Clearly we in Canada must rationalize a new export policy. We must have one that is sensitive and subordinate to the whole of our national needs, and one that is part of a reasoned, systematic approach to national development.
Above all we must realize that the empire building in the EDC, empire building for its own sake, must be brought to rein in the face of broader and more beneficial national goals.

I say this is especially true in light of the bill we are now considering. This $27 billion package would enable the EDC to finance a growing number of contracts to countries that have the commercial and financial wherewithall to finance these projects for themselves. Increasingly, Canada is becoming a source of ready and cheap money, and increasingly we are subsidizing our exports, not merely supporting them. What is even worse, we are subsidizing our exports at the expense of vital needs right here at home.
In every corner of Canada today there is a crying need for the very type of projects that the EDC is now financing abroad. For example, in the maritimes, and I think some of our maritime colleagues will be speaking on this, there is a great need for a new fishing fleet to keep abreast of the highly competitive and highly technological fleets from other countries. Many millions of dollars a year, spread over a certain period down there, would go a long way to helping out our maritime fishing fleet.
In Vancouver, out in my area, we are in dire need of dry dock facilities which would be capable of handling today's modern ships. Some $100 million would go a long way toward providing this, plus a new light rapid transit system for the city of Vancouver.
Highways, railroads, and communications systems are needed in the north to open up Canada's vast lands, especially along the route of the proposed pipeline. Approximately 600 miles of the pipeline route are without telephone or television, and a lasting communications system would become a reality if there were an investment of $100 million.
Some 300 miles of the Alaska Highway require paving in order to create a viable tourist industry in northern British Columbia. Once again $100 million would go a long way toward accomplishing that.
Looking to the east, Montreal is desperately in need of a modern waste treatment facility. It has been considered many times, but the project has gone through a number of convolutions and appears to be threatened again because of the lack of money.
In other cities in the country, virtually every public transit project plan is in trouble because of financial shortages.
These examples, and scores of others, illustrate the kind of development we in Canada could foster if we applied the EDC approach right here at home. Why not let the EDC be transformed into a national development corporation whose chief task might be the development of the infrastructure, such as these fishing fleets, grain elevators and so on, so necessary if we are to realize our true potential in Canada today? The new national development corporation could absorb the export functions of the Export Development Corporation, which would continue pretty much as before, with one major exception-export contracts underwritten by public funds would be weighed for the contribution to long-term national goals, such as the creation of permanent jobs and their protection of Canadian industry. It would not be much different than the method now used by the government under the Foreign Invest-

ment Review Act where there is a committee which considers the prospects of foreign investment and weighs it compared to other investments for substantial benefit to Canada, and if it passes the test then it is allowed. A similar test could be applied by this new development corporation to determine whether Canada should finance projects overseas.
This new national development corporation would loan low cost, long-term money to provinces, municipalities, and other groups which could not obtain private financing for their projects. High priority could be given to those projects which contributed to fortifying the economic base, especially those projects which would act as a catalyst in inspiring other development in the private sector.
The chief advantages to establishing such a corporation are these: first, it would help to rationalize our export policy by continually weighing our support of exports against domestic needs. Secondly, it would provide a cheap source of funds for the development of Canada itself, with all the attendant bonuses of higher employment and a stronger economy. Thirdly, it could be instrumental in bridging the five to ten year slump in the 50-year cycle of capital expansion that we now seem to be experiencing. Fourth, if both the CDC and the EDC were merged into a new national development corporation, a new economic strategy for Canada could be formulated which would balance our exports and industrial objectives. Finally, if a new export policy is thus rationalized, private Financial institutions could be encouraged to contribute to a fund for the development of third world nations on the threshold of development. A new foreign development corporation could be established with a working fund of perhaps $1 billion.

Today I look at the Export Development Corporation, and specifically at Bill C-36, with mixed feelings. Just what does Bill C-36 accomplish? It increases from $8.85 billion to $26 billion the capacity of EDC to finance, insure, and guarantee export contracts. Under the present act there is an insurance ceiling of $3.5 billion, including $1 billion for government account; under Bill C-36 there will be an increase to $13.5 billion, including $3.5 billion for government account. Under the present act there is a loan limit of $5.1 billion, including $850 million for government account; under Bill C-36 there will be an increase to $12.5 billion, including $2.5 billion for government account. Under the present act there is an investment guarantee of $250 million, and under the new act that guarantee will be ten times the present incorporation, or something like $10 billion. Under the old act the total is $8.85 billion, and under the new act it is $26 billion.
We have to ask ourselves what EDC has done with its money in the past and what projects it has established. In a press release dated February 8, 1974, EDC announced it would put up $132.5 million for an integrated forestry complex in Iran; on October 14, 1976, it announced loans totaling $102 million for a pulp and paper mill in Poland; on September 21, 1977, it announced $1.8 million for a pulp and paper mill in Peru; on November 8, 1977, $102.6 million for a new pulp and paper mill in Iran; December 28, 1977, $5.5 million for a pulp and paper project in Romania; March 8, 1978, EDC announced loans totalling $57 million for two pulp and paper projects in Argentina. The total of EDC money going to foreign pulp and paper concerns amounts to around $401.4 million, not counting at least three projects announced by EDC in press releases since February, 1978. These pulp and paper projects are part of EDC activity totalling $600.97 million.
I point this out to the House because, if my memory serves me correctly, the Canadian pulp and paper industry is working

In view of the Prime Minister's past changes of parliamentary rules, which have virtually destroyed parliament's control of government expenditures, I submit that we should not be too anxious to let this man tamper with our constitution.
Obviously we must alter course. We must change our direction in so far as our economic policy is concerned. Some of the old concepts which have put us so deeply in debt during the past decade under this government must be questioned. No one in his right mind would agree they are working. We need to show more concern for the small businessman. We need to show more concern for business in general, for our farmers, for our fishermen, and for those who work, as we say, at the grass roots level.
I am not proposing in this speech that we abolish the Export Development Corporation. It is obvious that some of its aids programs are more political than economic. For example, aid to Cuba and to other foreign communist countries in the form of loans totalling $375.5 million in 1976 must surely be put to question in light of the agressive stance taken by Cuba, backed up by Soviet war equipment, on the continent of Africa. We have too small a population in Canada, some 23 million people, to be indirectly involved in a war of aggression on the African continent. I submit that loans of this magnitude would be more productive if they were made to Canadians for developments in this country.
Perhaps the time has arrived when we should consider the establishment of a maritime commercial development corporation. This idea is similar to the one proposed by the preceding speaker, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke). In this instance I am talking about a Canadian organization, an organization which would be dedicated to assisting development in Canada, assisting in the establishment of jobs on both coasts of Canada.
Quite frankly, I disagree with the minister when he says perhaps the Polish people can build ships better than Canadians. This apparently was his statement in this House on Friday. The Poles do not agree with him either. Four cargo ships were built recently for Polish ocean lines at Sorel, Quebec.
I would point out to the minister that the inherent importance of maritime concerns to the entire Canadian nation cannot be underestimated. Three impressive ocean coastlines and a massive inland water network impinge on the daily lives of virtually all Canadians. "A mari usque ad mare", "From sea to sea" may in retrospect be slightly restricted because Canada does not end at its coasts. Our continental shelves occupy more than one million square miles of territory, or one third of the Canadian land mass. Because of this fact I would
April 24, 1978

point out that the importance of maritime industries, and especially transportation over water, is in no danger of declining in the foreseeable future. No other mode comes close to offering an economic alternative to the movement of bulk goods over great distances. So we are on safe ground in a very uncertain period if we, as a government and as a country, encourage its development.
The shipbuilding industry has always catered to the needs of the conventional deep sea trade, the defence sector, and the fishing industry. However, vast new frontiers are beginning to emerge, providing challenges that boggle the mind. Harnessing the ocean's energy, Fundy tides, harvesting mineral nodules, exploiting petroleum reserves, gas reserves, and even the cultivating of new food sources from the sea, all provide new challenges for today's society, in particular for maritime industries.
These opportunities will not remain as visions of the future forever, but to capitalize on them will require changes in the nature of our maritime industries. Especially do we need changes immediately in the attitude of this government. We need them now.
If we are to cope with the future, we need only to travel back in our imagination a single lifetime, say to the year 1900, to realize how much of today's technology would be not merely incredible but incomprehensible to the keenest technical brains of that time. We are therefore, in my opinion, wasting valuable time.
In spite of all that has been said by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc), we need the immediate development of a freezer trawler fleet if we, as Canadians, are to capitalize on the extensive fisheries markets that are open to us in Japan. These markets are fantastic. That is not my view alone. I quote from a recent article:
Mitsunori Yoshida, a representative of Japan Fisheries, says the Canadian fishery offers a "great hope" for his countrymen wh annually consume more than 10 million metric tons of seafood.
Fish supply in Japan this year has been cut by almost 40 per cent because of the various declarations of 200-mile limits throughout the world and particularly in the Soviet Union, the United States and Canada.
Yashida said not only does Japan want to buy more than a proposed 300,000 tons of Canadian fish annually by 1985 but it also wants to establish a series of co-operative fishing ventures in Canadian waters. Japan is currently dealing with the Canadian government in an attempt to establish those fishing ventures.
According to Charles Moulton, president of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway Transport and General Workers Union: "There is no doubt in my mind that if we are to service these markets we must get started on development of our own freezer trawler fleet."
"We have been afraid of the U.S. market which traditionally has always been our biggest buyer. We must make plans to find other export markets and in preparation for it we must have the freezer fleet."
What bothers Moulton now is that everyone is talking about a freezer trawler fleet but "no one is doing anything about their construction."
That gives some indication as to what opportunities are available to us. It is obvious that our fishing fleets on both coasts must be mechanized and modernized within the next ten years. Experts estimate this will result in approximately $1 billion in new work in our shipyards. However, to assure this
Export Development Act
future, it is necessary that the shipbuilding industry remain healthy during the next two or three years in preparation for the challenges and opportunities of the 1980's.
A maritime commercial development corporation operating for Canadians would, in my opinion, go a long way toward re-establishing our Canadian shipbuilding industry. I hope these views are kept in mind before we place too great an emphasis on expanding the Export Development Corporation. Let us not continue as we have in the past decade with the destruction of Canada. Let us get on with the job of reconstructing Canada. A viable shipbuilding program along the lines I have proposed, and for the purposes I have outlined will,
I submit, go a long way toward bringing about this objective.

Mr. Speaker, my participation in this debate is motivated by a concern for the economy of this country. We hear the argument, and it was put forward by the minister when he introduced this bill on Friday, that the whole purpose of the Export Development Corporation is to ensure that Canadian industry is put in a more competitive position than it would otherwise be for export. That is one reason. The other reason puzzles me now and puzzled me last Friday afternoon when another bill was put forward dealing with gold coinage.
I am puzzled by the urgency. This was mentioned by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) and also the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke). What is it that brings this bill before us at this time? We have good cause to ask why this bit of patchwork, if it has been in the mind of the Export Development Corporation for all these months, as it appears it has been, why did they wait until these last few days to see if it would be possible to have it rushed through at the last minute?
My concerns here are with this government's sense of priorities. We have seen our national debt double within the past ten years ago. Our deficit equals what budgets were ten years ago. Interest on the public debt has increased by five times, and per capita interest charges have almost quadrupled in the past ten years. These are indicators of a very serious economic situation in our country. Why has the government not put forward a comprehensive program to remedy the situation that I am sure even they admit exists today?
In 1968 unemployment was something in the order of 375,000. Today it is over one million. It has almost tripled in ten years. This is a serious problem. What we get is just one component. True, it is an aspect of our economic situation, but not the main aspect or main corrective of the situation.
Why is this government prepared to face the popular vote at this time without a comprehensive economic policy which will deal with our inflation, and with the problem of unemployment which is so serious in our country today? Therefore, I ask about the matter of the urgency. I want to deal with another aspect of the bill, but I am afraid that I will now have to call it five o'clock.

April 24, 1978
