speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first thing apparent with regard to this matter was in the words of the officer at the Table who indicated that the motion stands in the name of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, and is seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg
[Mr. Munro (Esquimalt-Saanich).l
North Centre (Mr. Knowles) of the New Democratic Party. Indeed, the measure we are talking about is of such a nature that, as I hope all hon. members will agree, it transcends party lines. I trust, therefore, that the motion will be supported by all members of the House of Commons.
It is important we should note that the purpose of the proposed subcommittee is-
-to investigate and report on the needs of Canada's physically and mentally handicapped citizens; in order to provide a basis of information, necessary in avoiding the current costly duplication and overlapping of services, and essential in planning legislation for a comprehensive program of services at the federal, provincial and municipal levels of government to support and supplement the excellent work of voluntary organizations; all with a view to making it possible for the handicapped to live a creative, fruitful and independent life in the family and community, and thereby placing Canada in a position of leadership in the rehabilitation movement in preparation for the XIV World Congress of Rehabilitation International to be held in Winnipeg during June 1980.
This motion is important because we all know how time slips by-we are almost in the middle of 1978 and there is a prospect that some time later in the year we shall be facing a general election. The lead time may be so compressed as to prevent adequate preparation. In the meantime there has been placed before the House of Commons a report, tabled by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), on the employment of physically and mentally handicapped people in the federal public service. This is a report of a Public Service Commission and Department of Manpower and Immigration study team, and it is dated September 6, 1977. The authors are Virginia C. Miller and Helen J. Morton.
Anyone who is interested in the position of the handicapped in the Public Service and of the proposals with respect to them, anyone interested in this plan to improve the opportunities available for them to live a creative life within the community, within the spirit of this motion, should read this report. I commend the President of the Treasury Board for arranging to table it in the House of Commons. It deals with the handicapped in a way which is almost undeniable. I also commend the government for deciding to increase the opportunities for the employment of the handicapped in the public service and for the statement issued by the minister under date of March 21, 1978. I commend the minister because, as I say, this is a subject which is above the daily clamour of partisan politics. It is an area in which action could be taken not only in the private sector but in the public sector.
In the public sector there is an opportunity for the federal government, regardless of its political stripe, to provide leadership. I think it important that the following statement in the document of March 21, 1978, be placed on record in relation to this debate:
The position of the federal Public Service should be summarized as follows: With respect to physically handicapped persons and without regard for the nature of the handicap, it is the policy of the government to provide, and to actively promote, equal access to employment and career development in the federal Public Service in work for which they are considered to be qualified and to ensure that any barriers to such equal access, whether procedural, attitudinal or physical, are progressively eliminated as quickly as possible.
April 24, 1978

With respect to mentally handicapped persons, it is the policy of the government to promote actively the increased employment of such persons within the federal public service in work for which they are considered to be qualified, and to ensure that where necessary special measures are utilized in the staffing process to give appropriate recognition to the nature of their handicap.
That is the statement made by the President of the Treasury Board, and it is one which members of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition support. Mr. Speaker, this report is so far reaching that it should not be tabled in the House only to be set aside. If we establish a committee and refer this matter to it, the objective of my hon. friend from Brandon-Souris, we ought to ensure that this report goes before that committee for consideration. I would therefore move, with the concurrence of my hon. friend from Brandon-Souris, seconded by my friend, the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro):
That the motion be amended by adding thereto the following:
"and the document entitled "Employment of Physicaly and Mentally Handicapped People in the Federal Public Service" should be immediately referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs for reference to the subcommittee."
The availability of this document can only enhance the work of the committee and increase the appreciation in the House and the country of the problems facing the handicapped. I hope this amendment will be accepted by the House.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION SPECIAL SUBCOMMITTEE INVESTIGATE NEEDS OF HANDICAPPED CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to oppose the motion or contribute to it being talked out, but I should like to make a few comments and contribute a few facts and ideas which I believe to be important for the record.
I am sure each and every one of us sitting in this chamber today will agree it is the right of every handicapped individual in this country to "live a creative, fruitful and independent life in the family and community", to quote the motion.
This is especially meaningful as it relates to the area of employment. As our society presently functions, employment provides the framework within which to earn not only a financial livelihood, but also to feel a part of the maintstream, to be "where it's happening." Akin to this, perhaps just as important, if not more important, is that work fosters confidence, the desire to achieve, and the satisfaction of accomplishment. I think hon. members will agree that these observations are true for everyone. What apparently was not officially recognized until relatively recently was the fact that they are just as true for the physically and mentally handicapped members of our society.
The recognition that there have been disadvantages for the handicapped in Canada with respect to employment resulted in the drafting of the Human Rights Act, section 15. Section 15 deals especially with the elimination of disadvantages suffered by those who are physically handicapped, and I quote:
It is not a discriminatory practice for a person to adopt or carry out a special program, plan or arrangement designed to prevent disadvantages that are likely to be suffered by, or to eliminate or reduc disadvantages that are suffered by, any group of individuals when those disadvantages would be or are based on or
Handicapped Citizens
related to the race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, marital status or physical handicap of members of that group by improving opportunities respecting services, facilities, accommodation or employment in relation to that group.
The same recognition was given in a recent study by the Employment and Immigration Commission and the Public Service Commission entitled "Employment of the Physically and Mentally Handicapped People in the Federal Public Service." I think that has been referred to already.
When tabling the document the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) outlined the government's plans for increasing opportunities for employment of the handicapped in the federal public service. I would like to read from that report. It is entitled "Government's Plans for Increasing Opportunities for Employment of the Handicapped in the Public Service."
Increased opportunity for the handicapped is clearly a matter of importance to the government. In 1975, Canada sponsored a declaration on the rights of disabled persons which was subsequently adopted by the United Nations General Assembly. That declaration specified that 'disabled persons have the right, according to their capabilities, to secure and retain employment or to engage in a useful, productive and remunerative occupation and to join trade unions'.
In that declaration the government was asserting that the right to work is not a privilege reserved for the non-handicapped. More recently, the passage of the Human Rights Act reiterated this concept by specifically prohibiting discrimination on the grounds of physical handicap and, moreover, explicitly recognizing the need for programs, plans or arrangements designed to eliminate or reduce disadvantages based on physical handicap.
We are all conscious that there have been disadvantages for the handicapped in Canada, and it was with this in view that, as Minister of Manpower and Immigration, the Honourable Robert Andras asked for a study of those disadvantages with specific reference to the federal public service. The minister wanted a frank and realistic appraisal of the kinds of problems which stand in the way of the handicapped when they seek employment or career development in the public service, so that these problems might be confronted head on and dealt with in a realistic way. That was the genesis of the report tabled this afternoon, which represents the combined efforts of officers of the public Service Commission, the former Department of Manpower and Immigration and a number of other departments.
The report, based on pilot projects, studies and widespread discussions with handicapped persons and associations representing the handicapped, was made available last year and provides us for the first time with a comprehensive view of the problem. What Mr. Andras wants to do now and particularly in view of his present responsibilities for personnel management in the public service, is to describe the measures which will be taken to address the problems which have been identified.
First, it is evident that much needs to be done in order to ensure that attitudes and employment practices do not discriminate against the handicapped. There is no deliberate discrimination; indeed, if there is any discrimination, it is quite unconscious and accidental. Nevertheless, if the concept of a non-handicapped person is what we have in mind when jobs or work places are designed, then the end result may very well favour the non-handicapped at the expense of the handicapped when employment decisions are made. Equally, if ignorance or misunderstanding is prevalent concerning the true capacities of the handicapped, then handicapped persons are likely to be overlooked when we search for candidates for many kinds of jobs.
What has to be done, therefore, is to attack these aspects of the problem on two fronts: first, the government must mount a vigorous information campaign within the public service aimed at radicating myths and misunderstandings about the abilities of the handicapped. In this connection, there is much evidence to demonstrate that the majority of handicapped persons are rated by their employers at least as high as, and often higher than, their non-handicapped counterparts in terms of such measures as punctuality, output, quality of work, attendance, stability and safety records. Handicapped people are good workers and it makes good sense to employ them. Through training and information programs, the government should ensure that all concerned focus on the

April24, 1978
Handicapped Citizens
capabilities of handicapped persons rather than on any real or perceived limitations.
Secondly, a vigorous program of change must be established with respect to policies or practices which unconsciously reflect some wrong attitudes. For this purpose, it is the government's intention that all its departments begin immediately to review and systematically eliminate any of their practices governing the design of jobs, the selection, training and career development of employees or the provision of office facilities and equipment which might discriminate against the handicapped.
The Public Service Commission has begun to examine its staffing policies, to ensure that handicapped persons are not inadvertently being screened out by recruitment and selection procedures which were basically designed for the non-handicapped: the way jobs are advertised, for example, or the manner in which job interviews are conducted. Thus an important task for the Public Service Commission will be to design recruitment and selection programs which are appropriate to the handicapped population, including the mentally handicapped. The Department of Supply and Services is already studying an expansion of the employment of physically and mentally handicapped workers in the provision of services and materials to the government. To facilitate that activity, the Secretariat of the Treasury Board is currently reviewing contract policy governing the use of sheltered workshops.
There are, of course, many other important areas in which the Treasury Board is or will be active in support of greater opportunities for the handicapped. Innovative approaches to job design will be considered, particularly where self-supervision, part-time employment, job sharing or work at home are concerned. Some of these have already been experimented with, with good results, and they can be applied successfully where handicapped persons are concerned. The Treasury Board will also look at its policies governing the provision of special equipement, so as to ensure that handicapped persons are not excluded from work for want of a mechanical aid or a piece of furniture adapted to their needs. It seems a small thing to a non-handicapped person, perhaps, but the lay-out of furniture or equipment in an office can be a real impediment to a person confined to a wheelchair.
All these activities are already under way or can begin immediately. They are activities which will be of great benefit to handicapped persons who are public servants or are seeking employment in the public service. They will be done as quickly as possible. Accordingly, all departments will be asked to start immediately on specific action plans for these activities, to report progress regularly and to hold managers accountable for the results achieved. Recognizing that these plans will profit from the advice of persons with special knowledge of the problems of the handicapped, an advisory group is being established, drawn from various agencies and associations concerned with the needs of the handicapped.
What has been described so far is a range of activities which will promote the changes in attitudes and pratices necessary to open up the public service to handicapped persons. It is a fact that there are some real problems with respect to physical access to government buildings or to their internal facilities. Many of these buildings, whether owned or rented, lack parking facilities, ramps, handrails, elevators or washrooms suited to the needs of handicapped people. While it has been a practice for several years to design appropriate facilities into new construction, or require them in buildings that might be leased by the government, there are many buildings which do not contain them but which still have many years of useful life. Conversion of these will not be cheap and in view of the government's intention to restrain spending the costs involved will have to be looked at carefully. Nevertheless, the Department of Public Works has been asked to co-ordinate studies of how to, by 1983, fully convert all government owned or leased buildings in which handicapped people might be employed. In establishing priorities within this plan the government will obviously bear in mind the need to accommodate not just public servants but also handicapped persons among the general public who need access to public buildings.
It is the government's intention to keep track of the results achieved in its programs and activities. This is a third major problem area, because the fact is that there has in the past been no satisfactory basis, in terms of either definition or statistics, for keeping track of our performance concerning employment of the handicapped.
With the promulgation of the Human Rights Act there is now a definition of a physically handicapped person which can be used in the employment context. For working purposes, the definition of a mentally handicapped person which the

authors of the report proposed has also been accepted. However, neither of these would be of very much help without statistical information concerning the numbers of handicapped persons who are working or who have applied for work in the public service.
I would like to have read the rest of that report. It is an excellent report and it would be worth while having it on the record, but I would like to stop short of quoting it further. I think all of us in this House can see the sense of responsibility and action in that report. I would now like to sum up quickly by saying the following.
As most hon. members are now aware, a block financing proposal has recently been made to the provinces to cover the costs of social services, including transportation services for the disabled. It represents the substituting of one financing arrangement, namely, block funding, for another, the conditional shared cost arrangement associated with the new social services legislation, Bill C-57.
As you may be aware, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) met with her provincial colleagues on March 6 and 7, 1978, to discuss the federal government's offer to block fund social services in place of the conditional cost sharing approach contained in Bill C-57. As a result of that meeting it has been decided to implement the block funding arrangement effective April 1, 1978. The financial formula takes into consideration current expenditures on social services, an additional amount to provide for more comprehensive coverage, annual escalation based on changes in the gross national product and the population, and a levelling adjustment that would gradually eliminate, over a ten year period, the provincial differences above or below the national average contribution by Canada so that at the end of the period each province would be receiving the same per capita amount.
I should like to add that the federal government will be providing financial support for the same services that were identified in Bill C-57, services that had been agreed to by the provincial and the federal governments as being necessary in this country.
Since the provincial governments as well as the federal government have indicated a real desire to improve social services, and as the needs of the handicapped are a very real concern to the federal government and the provincial governments, I am confident that the new arrangement will result in the development of services designed to enable the handicapped to participate more fully in Canadian society.
The federal government realizes that as much as possible should be done for the handicapped. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has made it clear that she is dedicated to aiding, and indeed, is most anxious to aid, the disabled in their desire to leave the institutions, to achieve integration and to become full and contributing participants in Canadian society. All of us here will have a part in the achievement of this goal in our capacity as legislators.
For this reason it is my pleasure to commend the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) for having proposed this motion. It is the type of motion, the type of sentiment, which will focus the awareness of all members on
April 24, 1978

such things as barriers. If there is any uncertainty about the motion, it is about whether it should be dealt with by means of a subcommittee of the standing committee. I understand that we will soon be debating the block funding legislation.
One other possible alternative is that when this legislation is being debated by the standing committee, it might be an opportune time for the idea contained in the motion to be debated. To my mind, it would be useful to look at this motion again at that time in the context of all social services legislation.
In closing I would like to say that I think it is important for us all to take a very close and frank look at that motion.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION SPECIAL SUBCOMMITTEE INVESTIGATE NEEDS OF HANDICAPPED CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us today the motion standing in the name of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) that the House consider establishing a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs to investigate and report on the needs of the physically and mentally handicapped citizens in Canada. I should like to commend the hon. member for his motion because it affords us an opportunity to bring before the House of Commons the serious problem facing thousands of Canadian citizens, and an opportunity to try to prompt the government to take corrective action.
I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who seconded the motion, would have wished to be here today to follow the proceedings, but, as we know, he is in Winnipeg attending the funeral of his wife.
The problem of the physically disabled or handicapped is, I am sure, a problem that every member of parliament comes across during his term of office, in terms of people who come to the MP hoping they can be helped to become, to the degree possible, productive members of society.
I have had many examples of constituents who have come to me who do not qualify for any kind of federal, provincial or municipal assistance because they are not totally disabled under the definition contained in the various acts, yet at the same time suffer some kind of physical or mental disability which bars them from being employed. It is a sad experience to see another individual in that state of affairs, someone who desperately wants to fit back into society in some small way, in order to feel a part of society, rather than being shunted into some corner and not looked upon as a productive and full-fledged member of society. Many of them want to be able to participate in work in some way. We are so imbued with the work ethic in our society that people who are barred from working lose a sense of dignity and self worth. It is a very frustrating experience for them because they know they have talents and they would like to participate, yet they find some kind of barrier stopping them from taking part in society.
It is important that we understand and examine the extent of the problems of the handicapped and the disabled in our country. We have to begin, first of all, by working out a definition of "handicapped" or "disabled". We have a number of pieces of federal legislation on the books right now which do not have a common definition of "disabled". I refer, for
Handicapped Citizens
example, to the Canada Pension Plan which contains the disability provision and where disability is defined as being severe and prolonged. Yet, when you try to get that definition narrowed down further, it is at the hands of the bureaucrats and the regulations, and in the end it is defined as meaning you have to be fiat on your back or confined to a wheelchair.
There are many persons whom we as members of parliament see who, we know, under any rational definition of "disabled" would qualify, but, for the purposes of the legislation, they do not, and therefore they cannot receive assistance under the Canada Pension Plan.
Another example was brought to my attention recently by a constituent filling out his income tax form. There is a provision there allowing a deduction to be made by someone who is disabled under the provisions of the Income Tax Act. This particular chap was undergoing kidney dialysis. He had to spend two days a week in the hospital, or seven hours, undergoing dialysis, and a number of hours each day in bed at home recuperating. People who have read the little brochure that taxpayers get will have seen the provision which states that if someone has been confined to bed for a lengthy period, he qualifies for a tax deduction on the cost of these treatments. My constituent filled out the form and was granted the deduction for 1976. But suddenly he was disqualified on his 1977 tax return and has had to repay a lump sum. Anyone reading the brochure would have thought that person qualified, but according to Revenue Canada he did not.
The first thing we have to do is clarify and define in a consistent way and for the purposes of federal and, hopefully, provincial and municipal legislation just what we mean by someone who is handicapped or disabled. The second thing we have to do is begin to identify who are the handicapped and disabled in our society, who they are in terms of sex, age and location, so that we actually know how many handicapped people we have.
I made a very rough investigation through various agencies that deal with handicapped people and was astounded to learn the extent to which Canadians suffer from some kind of handicap or disability. I learned there are some 15,000 paraplegics in Canada and there are 13,000 people registered with the National Institute for the Blind. That institute estimates that in addition there are 75,000 Canadians with a visual impairment severe enough to cause employment problems. I also learned that there are some 266,000 Canadians suffering from serious hearing impairments and 50,000 known cases of mental illness requiring hospital treatment each year, with some 250,000 treated through out-patient facilities for mental disorders.
In fact, I was astounded to learn that over $1 billion a year is being spent on psychiatric services in Canada. I also discovered that we have at least 200,000 known alcoholics in Canada, and that on Canadian pension disability plans as of June, 1977 there were 64,600 people receiving disability benefits. I found out that in the province of Ontario alone the

April 24, 1978
Handicapped Citizens
workmen's compensation board is paying out 46,000 pensions each month to workers who have a work related disability. The figures begin to add up, not only in the thousands but in the tens of thousands. I do not think all the members of this House, or the public in general, realize the extent of people in Canada who have to undergo the discrimination or disadvantages associated with one disability or another.
The United States has done a study which estimates that one of every seven Americans is handicapped in one way or another. If we in Canada did a study I think the figure would be somewhat similar.
Therefore, I would recommend to members of the House that we should as a beginning step, in addition to the subcommittee, make sure that on the next census form instituted in Canada we include questions relating to how many Canadians are disabled and the extent of their disability. This would be a very efficient way of finding out just who in this country are handicapped.
Besides defining and identifying the handicapped we must move more vigorously in the area of preventing discrimination against the handicapped, especially in terms of entry into public and private places of business, but, more important, I think, in the field of employment. I had the experience of a young man about 20 years of age coming into my constituency office only a few weeks ago who told me he was seeking employment with the largest employers in Sault Ste. Marie, Algoma Steel, but was refused employment on the ground he was bowlegged. The doctor for Algoma Steel Corporation examined him and told him Algoma would not hire him because of that so-called disability which, in the doctor's opinion, could lead arthritic problems when he was older. The young man went to his own doctor to get his medical opinion. His doctor said he did not think that bowleggedness would be a serious problem in his later life or could lead to arthritis. I went to the personnel manager of Algoma Steel and presented the case. Although he was very sympathetic to my arguments, he said he had to stand by the decision of the company doctor.
There is nothing in Ontario labour law or the human rights act of Ontario, under which jurisdiction companies like Algoma fall, to which that man could appeal for the protection of his rights. We have to move rapidly and comprehensively in some of the anti-discrimination laws that exist throughout Canada to make sure that examples such as I have cited are not allowed to occur in the future.
We have to improve the human rights acts of the provinces as well as their labour codes. I wonder if we should not take a leaf from the books of some European countries which have established a quota system for large employers which requires that a certain percentage of their labour force must be people who have some sort of disability. I was interested to find out that about 3 per cent of the work force of DuPont, a large industrial firm, are handicapped. This amounts to some 1,452 people. Studies undertaken by the corporation have concluded that 90 per cent of these handicapped people are rated by the company as average or better than average workers. We should first destroy this myth that somehow the handicapped

are unreliable, not eager workers and do not have talents and skills to contribute to the work force. Studies in the United States and elsewhere have shown that, with certain accommodation and goodwill, the handicapped can be very productive members of our society.
Another recommendation is that the federal government co-ordinate its efforts on behalf of the handicapped. I would like to see a multidepartmental approach so that we could have national health and welfare, manpower and revenue get together in a co-ordinated effort to improve the situation for the disabled in Canada.
I would certainly like to see more assistance in terms of loans and grants to the many volunteer organizations which do such a tremendous job on behalf of the handicapped. The government should study very seriously a system whereby we would be able to subsidize the wages of the handicapped for certain employers. Again and again the message I get from the handicapped is that they do not want to do the little "make work" kinds of projects they often are offered in sheltered workshops, but would like to do meaningful and productive work just like their fellow citizens. Many employers, while they see the moral side of that argument, find in terms of pure economics that it is too risky to hire someone who is maybe a little bit slower in getting things done; but if we were able to subsidize some of those wages, especially for the smaller employers, it would go a long way to overcoming much of the reluctance of certain employers to hire handicapped people. I hope the government will take that idea seriously and at least try some pilot projects.
Lastly, we must have an immediate campaign to begin to educate the public about handicapped people. When I was first elected I had a certain state of mind in respect of what being disabled or handicapped meant. However, the more I met with handicapped and disabled people, the more impressed I was with their abilities and their attitudes. The message has to get out among the general public that we as a government have a responsibility in this regard, and this must be done through the media and other public relations methods. I have seen many examples in my own riding of injustice and wrongdoing, and I have felt very frustrated because I know there is no legal redress for these people. We must make some real improvements in terms of legislation.
I have also seen volunteers in our society do such a heroic job on behalf of the handicapped. We would not want to shut them out, but rather encourage their efforts. They can only do so much with limited manpower and limited funds. Any society that calls itself humanistic will realize that there is a positive role for government to play.
I think I have outlined some of the roles in terms either of legislation on human rights or financing that we could play to bring these fellow citizens more into the mainstream of Canadian life, thereby restoring their sense of dignity and worth, which is a claim that every Canadian citizen has.
April 24, 1978

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION SPECIAL SUBCOMMITTEE INVESTIGATE NEEDS OF HANDICAPPED CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few minutes of the time of the House to say a few words on this motion which, of course, I support. This motion asks the government to set up a special subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, to investigate and report on the needs of Canada's physically and mentally handicapped citizens, in order to provide a basis of information, necessary in avoiding the current costly duplication and overlapping of services.
I shall stop here, Mr. Speaker, because I believe the point of this whole question is precisely the misunderstanding between the three levels of government. To set up a sub-committee as recommended is all very well; to look into cases takes a long time and it could take another two or three years before a report could be presented. It often happens as well that the report that is finally produced comes out too late and is already obsolete.
I think we should perhaps look closer during this study because I am not against the establishment of this subcommittee. I think however that even if we make a study for the well-being of handicapped citizens, we should think of the immediate possibility to negotiate agreements between the three levels of government, municipal, provincial and federal, if we are to come to something more concrete.
Several people organized movements, and I can point out that there is in my area a good organization working for handicapped people. In my constituency we have small manufactures for the handicapped but unfortunately, we often see conflicts between the various levels of government. I remember the opening of a manufacture which employed about thirty handicapped people; the first year, it operated under the responsibility of the federal government through winter work, Canada Works or other federal programs, and everything was all right, although a few months was too short a period.
We have noted that six or seven months were a somewhat short period to complete a whole year, although they would make them eligible for unemployment insurance benefits and continue to be paid a salary. But I suggest that even with unemployment insurance benefits, a handicapped person cannot help feeling unhappy when he has known the satisfaction of receiving a regular pay cheque for useful work. It is not so much the salary a person receives that matters, Mr. Speaker, but the job a person does. A person feels useful to society. These people are greatly improved when we meet them again at work at the plant.
Frankly, I was somewhat like all other people who had never been in touch with this group of people who are more often than not ignored by society, but after a few weeks, I could see these boys, these girls and sometimes these older people who are entirely transformed and who replied, when I asked them
Handicapped Citizens
why they looked so delighted, that they finally considered themselves useful to society and that they could live at last like everybody else. We thought that giving benefits of some kind to the handicapped was enough and that they were happy: I suggest it is quite the opposite and that we make of them the unhappiest people in the world. When we let them play useful parts in their own region, spend their time in a constructive way, that is when they consider themselves true men and women.
And our stumbling block at the time when we launched that industry was that the second year both governments so overlapped that we received a federal and a provincial grant; a conflict ensued and the following year we received nothing. We did not know whether the federal or the provincial government was going to look after that group. It was actually the provincial government which did something because when Canada Works projects were submitted, we were told that the federal level could not intervene as this was not in its jurisdiction. Meanwhile, the handicapped were in the forefront of this war between both governments.
That is why I was saying at the outset that the crucial point today is not the study of the matter but the agreement. Whose duty will it be to act so that we can finally have a solid base from which to go and know who is responsible? That is what is interesting. I remember that the secretary of that group is also handicapped. The secretary, the foreman, they are all handicapped and they are not used to this conflict of jurisdiction. This was the first time they encountered it, and I had to explain to them that that was Canada, a conflict of jurisdiction.
Therefore, I sincerely hope, Mr. Speaker, that while we study this matter, as study we must to encompass the entire country, we first of all aid the movements that are already started in order to come to some agreement. There can be agreement between the provinces and the federal government, to help those groups and allow them to continue. Their little factory is now doing as best as it can, but they are barely making it with the revenues they are netting; if there were some form of assistance, like in the beginning, I think the operation would run much smoother and the handicapped would not have to spend 50 per cent of their time working and remain idle during the other 50 per cent.
I believe getting orders is not a problem for that small manufacture. What is lacking is money to operate the business, and without knowing what is going on elsewhere, I feel those are the problems which also happen in the other communities which started to be concerned about their handicapped people. Someone said earlier that we should know how many handicapped people there are.
Surveys have been done in my area and of course we have been stunned to see how many there were, because only a few of them were visible, most of them did not speak up, remained hidden in the house and did not dare show themselves. At the

April 24, 1978
Handicapped Citizens
time of the survey they were visited at home and persuaded to come out in the light, to speak up and realize that like everyone else they were human beings and had a right to a good life in keeping with their abilities and needs. It seems to me that a new interest has been stirred up in that group and that today, at least in my area, we know perfectly well the number of our handicapped and we hope to help them more over the years.
Once again, I want to insist on that point because it is very important, and I would like that both government levels, federal and provincial governments, get together with a view to doing something concrete and permanent for those handicapped people.

speechtext:
We have many problems with handicapped people. One is age, but there are many other diseases which are regarded as types of handicap. For instance, the second last speaker mentioned defects of vision. There are as well people with strokes, cerebral palsy, amputation cases, paraplegics, severe diabetics, people with congenital malformations and mental retardation, or retardation which is congenital or acquired. We also have psychiatric illness. All of these are handicapped people and up to the present there have been fairly well defined causes for their not being accepted in a place of work. A lot of them have also found it difficult to be accepted in society. Like healthy or so-called normal people, however, they have a great need to be accepted in society and to be allowed to do meaningful work, to have some way of expressing themselves and some type of creative outlet.
It is very interesting that we now find some mental retardation is due to diseases like German measles in pregnancy-an

innocuous disease but one which causes retardation if contracted in the first three months of pregnancy.
There has been a debate about schizophrenia. Freud thought it was due to mental aberration which either developed or was stimulated by some abnormal circumstance. We are finding out that it also has a physical background, and this is a breakthrough. We have had a preliminary report from the doctor who runs the Lakeshore psychiatric hospital in Toronto which shows that many of his chronic patients were people with renal disability. These kidney cases had to receive treatment by renal dialysis in order to survive and in the process of treating them the doctor was astounded to find that some people thought beyond help had recovered. Some even went back to work. I mention these things because they point out the necessity for continued work and research and for trying to make the lives of these people more pleasant and meaningful.
The opposition House leader spoke of the need for this subcommittee. In Welland I have had experience with a society which is helping the handicapped. It was started in Port Robinson and the other night they held a dinner which the Lieutenant Governor for Ontario, Pauline McGibbon, attended. I was unable to attend because of an expected vote in this House.
The country as a whole must show an improvement in its attitude toward the handicapped. We should also find some way of changing the architecture of places of work, public buildings, residences and all areas of the environment which make life so difficult for handicapped people. The Department of National Health and Welfare is extremely concerned about the problem. A great deal of work is being done by the committee but the old question of more committees and subcommittees comes up. Studies are being carried out now into the work of private agencies, citizens and provincial and federal governments; it is not that the government is averse to this particular subcommittee study at all. AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Horner that Bill C-36, to amend the Export Development Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, when I called it five o'clock I was explaining why I had some doubts about this bill being brought forward at the present time in current circumstances. It is only a partial solution to one of the great problems confronting this country, namely, unemployment. While the increase we are being asked to approve would contribute to the reduction of this unemployment by ensuring orders for our exports, I am persuaded that there are other ways in which we could proceed and I propose to say more about this later on. The proposal is that the credit potential of the Export Development Corporation be increased from $400 million to $1 billion.
Even when the Export Development Corporation was an export insurance scheme, Mr. Speaker, I wondered why it was not possible to get an accounting of the extent to which credits which have been extended are being paid back. I know that when credits have been extended and debts are repaid the money goes back into the consolidated revenue fund. But surely the corporation should be in a position to indicate openly the extent of the sums it was getting back from the credits it had extended so that there might be a roll-over scheme, a self-liquidating fund for its operation. At the present time, except for what appears in the annual report of the corporation it is very difficult to learn the extent to which loans are being refunded.
One would imagine that since 1964, when the corporation came into being in an earlier form, there has been a considerable return on the expenditures laid out. There ought to be a means whereby, through parliamentary approval, the corporation might, for example, ask in a particular year that 80 or 90 per cent of the funds returned in the previous year or two be made available for future operations by the agency. But that is not how it works. The way it works is for the corporation to come to parliament and seek to increase the amount which can be made available for export development.
Some of my hon. friends have mentioned countries to which lines of credit have been extended. Cuba has been mentioned. Among industries, the paper industry has been mentioned. I believe that either through CIDA or the EDC, or a combination of the two, there is a scheme whereby bagasse, as it is called, or the crushed Fibre of the sugar cane, instead of being burnt or otherwise destroyed, is being converted into a form of paper. Some Canadian papermakers have had a hand, I understand, in this enterprise.

April 24, 1978
Export Development Act
The criticism I make of this operation is that, through this assistance in its industrial development, Cuba is being freed to send troops throughout Africa, causing serious problems for established authorities there. We should examine this aspect very closely. We hear from some quarters the suggestion that we should not attach political considerations to the extension of assistance, but there is a kind of precedent for doing so. An embargo, for instance, is the application of political considerations, in a negative sense, and one is being applied against Rhodesia. So if political criteria are being applied and given expression by way of an embargo, why are political criteria not applied when it comes to the extension of credit or assistance?
Algeria is another country receiving assistance from the EDC. I remember trying to find out where the $1.2 billion line of credit at very low interest had come from. I had received a number of letters sharply critical of this $1.2 billion being made available. Algeria must by now be one of the wealthy countries, whether good use is made of that wealth or not. Almost from the first day of its independence it managed to conclude contracts across the Mediterranean with France for the sale of petroleum products. There is, of course, still a great deal of commerce in liquid natural gas across the Mediterranean to France and other countries on the north shore of the Mediterranean. Algeria is not a pauper by any means, and therefore one has cause to wonder why $1.2 billion should be extended as a line of credit to Algeria.
The other criticism of Algeria was, and still is, that it was one of the host countries to hijackers of aircraft. It was the one country to which many hijackers wished to be sent once they sorted out their problems with the countries in which the hijackings took place. In other words, Algeria was the host country to international criminals. Therefore, why should we extend a line of credit of $1.2 billion to a country which makes itself a haven for the criminal element in the international community?
I question that particular line of credit, and if this bill goes to committee I would certainly like to get a further line on this. I am sure I will be given a suave answer like "They are in need of it". There was one little aspect about Algeria which amused me when I visited there with the then president of the Canadian International Development Agency. This will lead into another comment I want to make.
One of the projects which had been organized by CIDA was a school which was set up in Algeria to teach Algerians how to run a merchant marine. My friend, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) would roar with laughter to think that Canadians would teach anybody how to run a merchant marine. We have difficulty persuading this government to create a merchant marine in this country, yet CIDA managed to find technical people from around the country to go to Algeria to set up the administration of a merchant marine in that country.
That brings me to the final point I had in mind when I rose to speak about this measure. This was mentioned by the hon.
[Mr. Munro (Esquimalt-Saanich).l
member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) and also by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). Surely in today's world and with the problems confronting Canada there must be some way of using the funds which we are being asked to give to the EDC to help Canadian industry help Canada. There is talk about assistance to fishing fleets.
I mention this in terms of extension of assistance to a merchant marine because we do not have one. We have not had one, unfortunately, for a number of years. We built up a fairly respectable merchant marine during the war, but gradually it was allowed to deteriorate. The hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay), who sits on the government side, has risen to speak about this. The hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) has also spoken about it. I have spoken about it as well. On the economic ground of what it costs to import and export the goods which we import and export, surely to goodness it stands to reason that there ought to be a merchant marine in Canada manned by Canadians and using ships which are built in Canadian yards. Our shipbuilding yards are withering away, and much of the shipbuilding technology which we built up during the war is virtually lost to us now. It is still there, but we are very near the critical moment, and funds should be made available for the creation of a merchant marine. It cannot be done in one year. It is a fantastically expensive operation, but a start should be made. I have said this in this House before. I probably referred to it, at least in passing, in my maiden speech, and that was almost six years ago.
The tradition of the sea is part of Canada. I think even my friend the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton) would agree that there are traditions of the sea even as far inland as Welland. They are good traditions which ought to be kept alive, yet we are allowing them to disappear and die. The hon. member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) would also agree.
Me especially.

However, we ought to think and continue to think in terms of real deep sea transport with large ships. We export in the order of $40 billion worth of goods a year, and, if my figures are correct, we import about the same amount, but all in foreign bottoms. We pay billions of dollars to send our wheat abroad. We arrange to sell it, and then we arrange for someone to pick it up and carry it away. Why we do not have our own ships to carry our wheat? How many millions or trillions of tons, gallons or barrels of oil do we import into this country, all in foreign bottoms? Some of them are Liberian, some Panamanian and some Japanese.
Why should we not make a start at building our own merchant marine to carry the trade which is the very lifeblood of this country? What we are being asked to do today is to build up a fund for the EDC to allow Algeria to dream up the idea of a merchant marine. We will send away our technicians so that Algeria can have a merchant marine. It is absolutely ludicrous that we should be creating a merchant marine for someone else when we are not doing it for ourselves. There are
April 24, 1978

shipbuilding subsidies in the estimates. I was able to get at the last minute only the 1977-78 estimates, but there was $65 million for shipbuilding in the estimate of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Some of that was for fishing vessels 75 feet in length. There was federal support for accommodation of a new shipbuilding assistance program which was an extension of the subsidy program administered by the Department of the Environment for patrol vessels and fishing vessels, but not for the carriage of trade. These other vessels are important and needed, but we also need vessels for the carriage of trade.
I have the suspicion that this matter has been brought in at the last minute just to fill in time. It could have been brought in earlier. We are under some pressure to make sure it gets through. I suspect that there is something behind this bill which I do not like. I have misgivings about the fact that there is not a clear story about the returns on the loans already made and on which I assume repayments are being made. I hope they are not all being forgiven. Some of them maybe. On political grounds I question whether EDC assistance should be extended to such countries as Cuba and Algeria; I cite only those two. There may be others, but those two are the most obvious. We seem prepared to assist others, but we are not prepared to confront the problems of unemployment and lack of self-respect in our own country which we ought to be able to do through an organization such as this.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased indeed to be able to take part in this debate on Bill C-36 because I believe very strongly that we need an incentive which will induce our producers to make the extra effort which is necessary to increase our export sales and thereby start to produce the additional jobs which our people-and especially our young people-need today.
Because of this country's great dependence on the United States market-we ship 70 per cent of our exports to that market-and the steady move of that country toward protectionism, the development of additional markets has become particularly necessary if we are to increase our volume of exports, or even maintain our present level of exports.
Making sales in other countries depends to a very large extent upon doing four things successfully: first, going abroad and making personal contact with potential buyers; second, finding out what is required to meet the competition in those markets; third, returning to Canada and producing a product which can compete successfully; and fourth, displaying the product effectively before potential customers.
The incentive I suggest would allow producers to write off 200 per cent of all expenses connected with, first, making sales trips abroad; second, displaying their products at foreign trade fairs; and third, any other expenses incurred in sales promotion in the export market in excess of those made in the base year, the year before the plan goes into operation.
Export Development Act
Not only would all such expenses be completely written off in the year when they are made, but a considerable cash bonus would accrue to the company for its additional sales promotion activities. The kind of incentive I have mentioned would greatly encourage the kind of activity which is essential if increased sales are to be made.
Another thing which the government should do to help increase the sales of Canadian products abroad is to organize fly-and-buy missions whereby the important buyers in the principal foreign markets would be brought to Canada once a year to see Canadian products displayed in giant trade shows in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver, and our heavy machinery in the factories where it is made across the country. Such operations have produced spectacular results where they have been used, and have paid for themselves many times over by the additional business which they have generated. I hope that the government will have the good sense to introduce such incentives in the very near future because not to do so would greatly jeopardize the increase in export sales which this country so badly needs.
