I do not know whether this point has been made. A year ago, on May 12, 1977, the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs considered Bill C-47, an act to amend the Export Development Corporation. At that time the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens)-a more dedicated, hard working and astute member of the House there is not-
Hear, hear!
-our financial critic, a man who is going to make a tremendous minister of finance-
Hear, hear!

-who is going to put it all back together once we get the government out, if there is an election this century-was questioning the president of the corporation in the committee. He said this:
... If we raise you from the $750 million to the $2.5 billion-
That is what they wanted last year, and we remember C. D. Howe's famous statement "What's a million?". With this crew it is "What's a billion?". The hon. member for York-Simcoe went on to say:
-how long do you project ahead that that new ceiling is going to be sufficient for you?

We have to cope with the existing business, the secondary rate of growth which topples out in this case-

This is typical Ottawa "bafflegab", you will notice, Mr. Speaker.
-and the fact that we are prepared, if and when this increased ceiling is approved, to start writing some front-end risks of performance bonds, frivolous call and cross liabilities, which the companies have been crying for for some time.
Who can understand what he is saying?
We anticipate that on these two counts the new ceiling we put forward will carry us, we hope, through the end of 1978.
So last year at the committee meeting, when the president was asked whether this would keep them going, he said "through the end of 1978". Now we have the minister, acting like a cry-baby in the financial pages of the financial press in North America, bawling, crying and moaning that if it is not put through, they will stop operating some time in 1978.
They better get their act together. Either the president of the corporation knew what he was saying in May of 1977 and the minister does not know what he is saying now-that is my preferred solution to the problem-or else the president in 1977 did not know what he was saying and the minister does know now. That is so unlikely as to make it beyond belief. We know the minister does not know what he is saying. He has not said a sensible thing since he became minister. A more puerile performance by a minister of this government has not yet been seen.
The president of the corporation then went on to say:
That is, it will give us ample time to come back to parliament when we hope to have a major revision of the statute on the lending side.
This is certainly a major revision; it is in the billions of dollars. It raises the authorized capital from $400 million to $1 billion. It raises the number of shares from four million to ten million. It raises the ceiling for all contingent liabilities from $2.5 billion to $10 billion. We are talking about billions of dollars, Mr. Speaker. This crowd has gone wild with power! They have come to this parliament and they ask to be given extra authority to raise the amount from $2.5 billion to $10 billion, and we do not even have a chance to scrutinize properly what this corporation is doing.
I went to a meeting of the public accounts committee where this corporation came before it. It was sickening to see a corporation that is able to lash out guarantees in the hundreds of millions in loans and credit-in excess of $1 billion-and we in that committee unable to really dig in and get any information. Grown men and women were given ten minutes to ask questions while the "bafflegabbers" you asked the questions of took up nine minutes of "bafflegabbing" in response to the questions you asked. That is the only scrutiny that this parliament has had as respresentatives elected to represent the Canadian people over this Crown corporation, and we are now asked to go on and give them the ability to make $10 billion in contingent liabilities, up from $2.5 billion, and to raise the ceiling for all contingent liabilities re the government account to $3.5 billion from $1 billion. Not on your life, Mr. Speaker!
April 24, 1978

We would be derelict in our duty were we to rush this through as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce wants.
We want an accounting, we want this corporation before a committee of this House and we want them put under a grilling, a real grilling. We want to see what they are doing. We want to see what they are up to. That is what we want to see, Mr. Speaker. We are not just going to walk this through because the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce thinks this is an election year and we are going to fall over and play dead while he raises to industry and business the spectre that before the end of the year the corporation may run out of credit facilities. It is not going to run out of credit facilities. It is going to run out of credit with us unless it comes before a committee of this House and lets us get right into the meat and potatoes of that corporation and see what it is up to and what they are doing.
Now, Mr. Speaker, just look at the provision for loan losses this outfit has that is dealing in the hundreds of millions and even billions of dollars. What have they got there for loan losses? This is an example of "bafflegab" gone berserk, Mr. Speaker. Their provision for loan losses you will see in their financial statement for the end of December, 1977, page 5. The provision for losses and loans receivable is $4 million; provision for claims in insurance in force is $5,026,000. These are minuscule amounts when you are dealing in the huge amounts they are dealing in. What is the answer? We are told this at page 9:
Provisions for losses are based on a review of collectibility of all outstanding loans to sovereign and commercial borrowers. In respect of this review, the corporation recognizes that the future economic and political conditions in some of the countries where the corporation has made loans are subject to varying degrees of pressures, some of which are unpredictable.
You can bet your "bafflegab", Mr. Speaker; you can bet it is unpredictable what they are going to do in some of those countries. Have you seen the list of the outfits they are lending to and the countries? There is not enough sovereignty in most of those countries to put in a glass of water.
They say:
Accordingly, delays in the repayment of principal and interest may well occur from time to time.
That is an astute prophecy!
In the case of loans made to sovereign borrowers-
Now we are going to get it right square between the old eyes. Here we were worried about our money and about the difficult conditions and delays that might well occur from time to time with the varying degrees of pressure. We were getting worried, but now we come to the punch line so we won't worry any longer, the soporific statements that put the minister to sleep. Oh, the minister loves to hear statements like this. He does not need to worry then about the EDC and their billions of credit. What is the statement? The statement is, Mr. Speaker:
In the case of loans made to sovereign borrowers, that is the governments of countries or their agencies, payment delays are not necessarily indicative of a future loss requiring a provision.
Export Development Act
Why not? Here is a sovereign that has defaulted-defalcated. They have said, "Buzz off, we can't pay you". We are not going to worry about that. Why not? It states:
Sovereign entities and their international financial obligations do not have commercial mortality-
They might not have commercial mortality, but they have got an awful lot of other mortality in the barrels of their guns, Mr. Speaker. In other words, they are going to exist whether they pay their bills or not. That is exactly what they are going to do.
Sovereign entities and their international financial obligations do not have commercial mortality, and the international system does not allow the unilateral denial of a sovereign obligation.
What bellywash! Did you ever hear the like of that, Mr. Speaker? International law does not allow sovereign entities to unilaterally deny their sovereign obligations. What a joke! All through the centuries they have done it tens of thousands of times, and the only way you can stop them is if you go in and invade, take them over and give them the iron fist.
Can't we see dear old Canada putting the iron fist to all these countries in Africa and South East Asia, not to talk about Poland? Suppose the Poles do not meet some of their obligations? Are we going to send the Canadian armed forces steaming over to Poland to show them that it is just not allowed by the international system for them to internationally spurn their obligations? What a laugh. Imagine this appearing in an official government document. It might have made the minister feel better but it does not make me feel better. I want this outfit before a committee where we can question them hour after hour, day after day and week after week until we find out what they are up to.
This is another quotation:
Furthermore, the international system provides several mechanisms and institutions through which countries facing repayment difficulties can effect remedial measures in agreement with their creditors.
Did anybody read about Indonesia a few months ago and how the whole shooting match just about went up the spout with their great company pertimax, whatever it is called, over in Indonesia which was unable to meet its obligations? All the great U.S. banks and others that have been lending all the money, and who pretend to know so much about international economic order, just about all went down with Indonesia and had to get together and kiss the old Indonesian whatnot so they would not go under. Because if they had gone under, they would have taken all of them with them. That is what is happening, Mr. Speaker. The creditor countries are afraid to collect. They cannot put any pressure on to collect because if they do the whole house of cards will come tumbling down. Then they state:
Therefore, except in the rare instance of outright repudiation or a write-off of asset value agreed to by creditors, in the opinion of management the ultimate collectibility of a sovereign obligation, and thus its asset value, is not subject to question although delays may have to be accepted.
Yes, delays-something like a thousand years. They do not want to put this in their accounts. They do not want to allow reserves for it. What is a thousand years in the life of a

April 24, 1978
Export Development Act
sovereign entity? Have you ever in your life, Mr. Speaker, had this kind of malarkey thrust before you in an official document?
Finally, if the review of the outstanding loans does not specifically indicate future loss, it is the policy of the corporation nonetheless to set aside each year some provision in consideration of the total loan portfolio.
Something like $1 for $100 million, I presume, because they certainly do not show much allowance here.
I am only giving the House this example, not because I want to denigrate the Export Development Corporation, but because I want to get them on the right track. I want to get them under the scrutiny of the people who are elected to this parliament to govern these things. Because in twenty years' time, or thirty, they will be looking back to see what we did and how we acted with this corporation that is now so proud of itself, and so boastful about itself, and which so easily gives away billion dollar credits around the world.
There is an oil refinery in Come-By-Chance, Newfoundland, that was not financed by the EDC because it is in Canada. They are not financing or helping with development anywhere in Canada in the underdeveloped areas. No, that is one of the things that is wrong. We should have a credit agency that does that. That oil refinery in Come-By-Chance was financed by the ECGD, the English export credit department of the board of trade which is the equivalent in England of the Export Development Corporation here.
I remember Mr. Smallwood saying how the ECGD had said the whole thing at Come-By-Chance was feasible and economically sound, and that is why nobody should question it. I had the temerity to question the deal; I had the effrontery to question the great wisdom of the deal at Come-By-Chance. I got jumped all over for three years, and brutalized politically, but I fought back, Mr. Speaker, and here I am ten years later and I am still going to speak my mind and expose this kind of chicanery whenever I come across it.
They went ahead and ECGD financed it, and they are holding the bag for $110 million today. That is what ECGD is doing because they are interested. And so the EDC; they are interested in financing Canadian exports and it is, very, very secondary whether the credit they are giving is sound or not. They are not concerned about how sound the credit is. They are not concerned. They want to have a big record. Mr. MacDonald wants to come before the committee and say: "We had a billion dollars; we whacked out a billion dollars last year in credits. We financed a billion dollars worth of exports."
The January/February "EDC News" states in the heading, "EDC Loans Top Billion Dollars in 1977". That is what they want, another record, not whether the $1 billion in loans is sound from a banker's point of view. They are interested in financing and their job is to finance Canadian exports and to help us export more. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, they are prepared to take risks and they are taking risks that bankers would not take.
They are going to get stung with big losses, Mr. Speaker. The losses that ECGD are suffering in Come-By-Chance, Newfoundland heralds the losses that EDC are going to have the way they are operating around the world. Mark my words. I do not know how long it is going to take, a year, five years, ten; but they are going to suffer some big, staggering losses. You can see it there now. They have got huge outfits like Inco who have gone ahead in Indonesia, and Falconbridge in other parts of the world, in nickel mines. They compete with their own nickel mines over here where they are having big problems now because of the economic conditions of the world, the demand for nickel has gone down, and so on. And these are large projects that one would normally think there would never be any trouble with. The whole thing is a shaky edifice, Mr. Speaker. We can only hope that in the next or 24 months it is not going to topple.
I have another point to make with this EDC. They had the unmitigated audacity, Mr. Speaker, the unmitigated gall as a Crown corporation-this House should take notice of this and put them in their places-to say this in their "EDC News", January/February, 1978. I turn to page 2 and I see "EDC answers MPs charges". Then they say in an article that recently appeared in a number of local newspapers:
Conservative MP William C. Scott (Victoria-Haliburton) called for the abolition of EDC and charged that it was a "threat to the future of some of (Canada's) domestic industries".
And then EDC went on to answer what they said were the hon. member's charges. He identified Mr. John Bowles, EDC's director of corporate communications, and he identified four statements that he said were particularly misleading. Then there is practically a whole page answering what they said were charges by a Conservative MP.
What is this outfit doing, having the audacity and the gall, Mr. Speaker, to interfere in our political life and to criticize what a Conservative MP had to say about them? That is the job of their political master, or their supposed master, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. How dare they take it upon themselves in their "EDC News", to attack a Conservative MP. The minister should act on this. There should be people dismissed for this. It is the minister's job. If the minister does not agree with what the MP from Victoria-Haliburton said about the EDC, it is up to the minister to respond, not the EDC.
I am surprised and shocked, Mr. Speaker. As far as I know this has not been brought up before. I have not had a chance to bring it up. We have not had them before a committee, or at least not a committee that I have been at. If this was a Liberal MP, Mr. Speaker, do you think this outfit would dare criticize a Liberal in their "EDC News"?
No.

No way. If a Liberal MP had made some criticism of the Export Development Corporation, do you think that they would have had a page in their "news", paid for by the taxpayer, and if they would have answered the MPs

April 24, 1978

charges and named him a Liberal? If they ever come out with an article while this government is in power saying "Liberal MP Smith said this, that and the other and he is all wet and he is all wrong", that will be your day, Mr. Speaker.
I am asking the government for an explanation for this. Who was reprimanded for this? Here are civil servants of a Crown corporation-all right, they are not civil servants, but whatever they are, employees of a Crown corporation-putting out a newsletter criticizing a Conservative MP. Is it the policy of the government that Crown corporations are now free, holus-bolus to criticize and attack members of the opposition if the members of the opposition make statements that they do not like? Is this House going to put up with this, Mr. Speaker? I dare say it will, the majority are Liberals, and this plea will probably fall on deaf ears. The minister is not here tonight.
As for the EDC, well, I will not go into the criticism they made of the Conservative MPs statements that they said were particularly misleading. One of the statements that the hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton made was this:
EDC has gotten completely off the track ... loaned millions of dollars ... for the construction of nickel mills in countries (competing with) Canadian nickel producers.
How is that misleading, Mr. Speaker-"particularly misleading", Mr. Bowles said. It is not misleading at all, it is exactly the truth. EDC helped Inco and Falconbridge and others, or those two in any event, to construct nickel mines and mills in countries that compete with their mines in this country. That is the truth, and they got cheap financing from EDC to do it. This is one of our criticisms. It is not only our criticism, it is a criticism many people are making, and which the NDP party certainly made, of what the EDC is doing. They are giving cheap credit and easy financial terms to people who are going to compete with us all over the world, not just in nickel, but in pulp and paper. I can give all kinds of instances. There are two pulp and paper mills going into Argentina, another in Poland.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, we are a big export nation in pulp and paper, and if we are going to help to finance them in Poland and Argentina and everywhere else around the world, we are only helping to finance our competitors. They are going to go for export orders just as most of our industry has to go for it. To get temporary jobs in constructing the manufactured equipment and so on, are we going to help these people compete with us forever?
This requires intensive review to see whether it should be permitted any longer. It is a short-term game for a long-term detriment. So when the hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton made that statement, to think that this Crown corporation could call his statement particularly misleading and go on and answer it like this is just beyond belief. If that happened in Newfoundland, Mr. Speaker, with any Crown corporation, that would be it. They would be gone, dismissed, out. It just would not be permitted. This is a Crown corporation that has gone wild. They are only a different form of organization from the civil service. They are out in a corporation and civil servants are in a department. But they are still owned by the
Export Development Act
government, Mr. Speaker. They are in that forum that gives them a little more flexibility, but it does not give them political freedom. I am going to be calling on the government and the minister to take some action on this. Who has been reprimanded; who got demoted; who was dismissed; will it ever be permitted again?
There has been a $285 million line of credit extended to Poland, $46.9 million for goods and equipment for Poland's Kwidzyn pulp and paper complex and so on. Yes, we are asking questions about that because I think there is something peculiar about it.
Now, here is a mini steel mill being assisted to go down in the United States. This quote is in the March April "EDC News":
Sale of Canadian-produced mini steel mill will generate 1,350 man-years of employment.
This mill is going to go down in Perth Amboy, New Jersey. The Whitby based firm of Co-Steel International Ltd. and its subsidiaries are launching a similar venture in Perth Amboy. The equipment is to be built in Canada, and it is being financed by EDC and Canadian banks. The Raritan River Steel Company in New Jersey is going to operate the mill and is expecting to go into production in late 1979. It is going to produce 450,000 tons a year, tailored to supply the market for steel rod, wire mesh and fastener industries along the U.S. east coast from Maine to Florida.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether this mill will compete directly with Canadian mills or not which export to the United States. Surely, if we are in the steel business, we have steel mills that make the same kind of product, yet here we are helping to finance a steel mill down in the United States.
A year or two ago when the present Minister of Finance was minister of industry, trade and commerce he said in Hansard, October 21, 1977, when this criticism was brought forward- and I quote the Minister of Finance who was then the minister of industry, trade and commerce; there have been seven of them in the last seven or eight years:
We are preoccupied with creating some growth for the poor around the world.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if that is the rationale, is the United States in this category? Is Canada so rich that we now consider the United States and New Jersey to be poor and we are creating some growth for people down in Perth Amboy, New Jersey? What malarkey! It is not what they are doing at all. The minister then might have felt that arrogance and so on about Canada, but he does not feel that way today with the trouble he is having with the Canadian dollar and all the rest of it.
We are concerned about what EDC is doing. We are not voting them additional billions of credit, Mr. Speaker, to go on this path until we see just what they are up to, until we get clear statements from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, who is going to commit them to go on as they are.
Now, here is an issue, January/February, paid for by the taxpayers, with two pictures of the Minister of Industry, Trade

April 24, 1978
Export Development Act
and Commerce, one on the English side and one on the French side. Even if we are bilingual, Mr. Speaker, the pictures are not bilingual; you only need the one picture. But no, we have two pictures of the minister and Mr. John A. MacDonald, the EDC president. It is the same picture on both sides, the French side and the English side, to make sure nobody will miss it. One of the perils of being bilingual is that you might see two pictures of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce where formerly you would only see one. Is that necessary?
The March/April issue shows two pictures of Mr. MacDonald again signing various deals. What is going on? Are we going to have somebody else leave the civil service and jump into politics? Why all these pictures of the president of the EDC? I would not mind having this to send to my district, Mr. Speaker. I would like to get my picture in next month. I call on EDC now to have a couple of pictures of opposition MPs looking on while they are signing a deal so that we can send it out to our districts the same as all the rest of them do. We hope it will be a deal we can support as being a sensible deal.
Now, parliamentary review. The Auditor General has reported. By the way, Mr. Speaker, I've got so much material I wish I had the hours to speak that I need.
Just keep going. They will give you unanimous consent.

While the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce says that he wants this legislation to help Canadian businessmen and to help our exports, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan) are trying to shake the confidence of Canadian businessmen themselves. I read this quote the other day here in the House just to show the hypocrisy of it. The Minister of Public Works was speaking to the Prime Minister about Canadian business abroad. He told them it wasn't too good, that Canadian businessmen were not really cracking and were not doing their job. The Prime Minister replied, "Judd, amen." I hope the electorate are going to say amen to Judd too. The Prime Minister went on:
-that's the story I get in all the trips I have taken. We Canadians seem to lack the entrepreneurial spirit, lack that hustle.
That's the Prime Minister's view of Canadian businessmen, Mr. Speaker, his statist, elitist sentiments which he expressed two years ago on an unguarded New Year's Day. I don't know what happened. I don't know whether it was the Ontario liquor board that loosened his lips or what, but that is still what he believes, Mr. Speaker. All this cosying up to business in the last few months means nothing. The Prime Minister says that Canadians lack the entrepreneurial spirit, lack the hustle. If they do, it is because of this government, Mr. Speaker. They have been hamstrung by them, regulated to death by them, they have been scorned by them, they have been taxed by them, tied up in knots by them, been insulted by them, they've been verbally assaulted by them. And the final insult was to make the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the

gentleman who now holds that portfolio, show how much Canadian businessmen were thought of by the Prime Minister.
If the Prime Minister is right and there is no entrepreneurial spirit, no hustle in Canadian businessmen, they are a bunch of slackers, they are a bunch that won't get off their duffs to go get an export order, why should we give them all these billions of dollars through the EDC? Why should we raise their limit for guarantees from $2.5 billion to $10 billion? Not at all. Who is going to use it? There is no hustle, there is no bustle, there is no zeal, nobody getting up off their duff apparently. The Prime Minister is certainly not getting off his to call an election. Little Orphan Annie he is now. He is stuck with an election he has got to call and he doesn't know how to call it. There he was in Toronto over the weekend going to the Blue Jays baseball game. By God, he must want to win this election pretty badly!
Boo!
He got booed there too.

Mr. Speaker, I mentioned lack of parliamentary review briefly. Oh yes, the Auditor General's report. Before I come to that, let me deal with the financing of projects in Canada. Apparently credit is unlimited to finance things to go to Indonesia, to go to the Dominican Republic, to go to Zambia where the kwacha is now 26 per cent higher in value compared to the Canadian dollar than it was a year ago. We are ashamed to go Zambia any longer. You can't look a kwacha in the face if you go there with a Canadian dollar. Because of what has happened to our dollar in comparison to the kwacha, if you go there you have to go with some other currency.
What is kwacha?

The kwacha is the currency in Zambia. It used to be a lot less valuable in terms of the Canadian dollar than it is now. All over the world the Canadian government through EDC can finance projects-mines, mills, steel mills but it finances nothing in Canada.
Don't give me the old DREE malarkey. DREE is just a grab bag now for paving roads, building roads, a few water and sewer systems and things like that. We have to have an internal EDC that will help the underdeveloped parts of this country. It is just as good to us if we build up our own country and help finance mills, pulp and paper, whatever it might be in our own country, as it is to do it outside the country. This government stood by and allowed the Labrador linerboard mill in Stephenville to go under without one cent of help-not a cent, not a sou, not a nickel, not a kwacha. It wasn't in the right province, Mr. Speaker. I am not going to say what the right one is because the next thing they will say is, "He is a bigot." I say they are a spigot. If I am a bigot they're a spigot and they are pouring it only into certain parts of the country and outside the country. Now they want us to go and assist them in billions more for all kinds of areas around the world except our own. We want an internal development corporation.
April 24, 1978

That's what we want, Mr. Speaker. We want something like that, something that will be properly reviewed by the House.
When we looked at the estimates this year the government was very proud to state that there was a decrease in the estimates for the Export Development Corporation of $365 million. That was tremendous news-EDC wanted $365 million less. It was reduced from $425 million last year to $60 million in the estimates this year. Our hearts jumped as good Conservatives who want to restrain government expenditures. We were pleased and thrilled with this government until we saw that EDC planned to borrow the money this year from the private sector instead of borrowing it from the government.
What is the difference, Mr. Speaker? The EDC is the government. It is owned by the government and if the government is not legally obligated to meet its debts, it is certainly morally obligated and it is certainly going to have to do it as a practical matter. The government is responsible for EDC debts. If EDC borrows the money direct itself or borrows from the government, there is no difference. The Canadian people are still responsible to see that it is repaid. No Canadian government is going to allow a Crown corporation to go bankrupt or not meet its obligations. When EDC goes and borrows the money itself, the government is still behind it 100 per cent. They have to be. They might not be albe to sue the government, but in actual practical fact the government is responsible and will have to be responsible. It is an entirely false sense of security to think that anything was accomplished in that reduction of the estimates this year. They are now not going to borrow from the government or take from the government, they are going to borrow from the private sector. They are not bankers and they are not going to be cautious with it. We have seen how they operate. I already pointed to the example of the oil refinery in Come-By-Chance as to what can happen to things that appear to be in excellent credit.
Financing Canadian exports is only half the equation. If we want to help our position in the balance of payments-I am glad the hon. member for York-Simcoe is here tonight because if I get off base on any of my statements on finance or economics he can slip me a note so that I can recover my tracks. I want him to nod his head surreptitiously if I do happen to make a mistake so that nobody will see it or notice it.
As I see it, financing is only half the equation. We want Canadian exports, but if we are to do something about our deficit on the balance of payments on the international account there are several ways of taking action. Increasing exports is only one of those ways. We improve our situation in tourism, we travel less abroad, we encourage more tourists to come from abroad to travel in Canada. That helps. We stop borrowing so much abroad so we don't have to pay so much interest abroad, or pay as many dividends abroad. That helps. We stop importing so much.
This country, I think, is the largest importer in the world per capita of any country. I think 35 per cent of all manufactured goods consumed in Canada are imported. I don't see the hon. member for York-Simcoe disagreeing so I assume I remember
Export Development Act
correctly. It was about 35 per cent, Mr. Speaker. What we need in addition to exports is some import substitution. What we want is not only to be helping Canadian businessmen to export but to help them to replace a lot of the imports we are bringing into Canada. This has got to be our policy.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has no policy to help industry. It has no industrial strategy. In fact, one of its higher civil servants a few weeks ago said you couldn't have an industrial strategy in Canada, that it was nonsense to even start to try to have one. What has happened to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is that industry was smothered at birth, Mr. Speaker. When those departments were combined industry got smothered and the trade section has been the glamour boy ever since.
If you increase exports, that is all that counts. It does not matter if imports are being increased at a faster pace. We had a deficit of $4.2 billion in the current account last year. That does not matter because we increased our exports. Have you ever seen anything so feeble, Mr. Speaker? Fantastic tunnel-vision. We need a lot more than just increasing our exports. We have got to stop importing so much. We have to manufacture the stuff here, to substitute for the imports.
When a province like Quebec attempts to help its own industry, where they lost 30,000 jobs last year in furniture, footwear, textiles-I have forgotten clothing; did I mention clothing? When they want to help reverse that situation by giving themselves some tax relief, to encourage their consumers to buy more, to encourage the manufacturer to get back those manufacturing jobs they have lost-30,000 the government's own figures, this government's figures-what does the government do but place the iron heel of fiscal oppression upon Mr. Parizeau's neck.
Mr. Parizeau has a pretty thick neck. I do not know anything about his head, but his neck is pretty thick. He is resisting this pressure. We are all in this country together to help one another. Why is it, just because a province suggests something that the federal government has not originated itself, that the federal government has to say no and to use such false and flimsy arguments to say no to? Why is it that all the wisdom in this country is supposed to emanate from the heads of the 34 people we have in the cabinet?

There is a half up in the Senate, I think. The other place I mean, Mr. Speaker. We must observe the proprieties; I mean the other place where many of our members on this side seem destined for. If this election is held off for another few weeks there will be none of us left. If there are enough vacancies up there, we would all be there. Some of us will resist the siren call to the Senate. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) spurned that siren call to the Senate. He has more gumption in his little finger than all 33'/4 members of the cabinet.

Hear, hear!

April 24, 1978
Export Development Act

I am glad he is here tonight so we can say nice things about him while he is here and not just while he is gone. I did not think I would have a second chance to say what a great contribution the hon. member for Halifax has made to our political life-
Hear, hear!
-and how much we admire that hon. gentleman.
Hear, hear!

We only wish he was running with us to take his rightful place in the cabinet of Canada after the next election. Maybe we can persuade him to change his mind and run down in Mount Royal and trounce the Prime Minister right where it hurts, right in his own district. The hon. member for Halifax is now bilingual and he is ready for anything. The next thing he is going to learn is Ukrainian.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, I can see that-
Order, please. I regret to inform the hon. member that his allotted time has expired. He may continue with unanimous consent. Does the hon. member have unanimous consent?
Yes.
No.

Mr. Speaker, in joining the debate at second reading of this bill, I would first like to suggest to hon. members that the bill we have before us has a much more serious consequence than most members on the government side like to admit. It has become quite standard for this government to delay the introduction of a bill. Then, when they bring it in, if they feel they might be a little embarrassed about it they immediately start lobbying both through the press and through the various people in the private sector, that somehow or other the opposition is delaying passage of the bill.
With respect to the bill now before us, that must be denied point blank. There is absolutely no reason for the government to suggest that there has been delay in this parliament with respect to their bill to amend the Export Development Act. The fact is it was introduced for second reading only on Friday and this is the first full day that we have had an opportunity to speak about this important matter. I say important, Mr. Speaker, because some place the emperor and his cabinet on the other side have lost perspective in this country. When they took power the total federal government spending at all levels, including what they then regarded as Crown corporations, totalled less than $10 billion.
To bring this debate into perspective tonight we are being asked, if the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) had his will, to virtually rubber stamp a bill which

would give one Crown corporation of the federal government the right to loan, guarantee or insure obligations totalling $26 billion, or insure more than two and a half times the spending that the entire federal government engaged in the year before the emperor took power in this country.
Let us get that into perspective. That is the magnitude of the amount we are talking about tonight. When I say that, it would be pertinent to put on the record the explosion there has been with respect to export development activities in Canada. I say this because it is a motherhood thing for members in this House to say "Let us create employment"; we are all in favour of that. It is a motherhood thing to say "Let us create more export activity"; we are all in favour of that. But there must also be some perspective regarding how far the government of the day is warranted in binding the Canadian public with respect to certain export financing that to some degree we are not be paid for.
Let us be blunt about it. To create a year's employment in Canada today we are basically lending billions to foreign jurisdictions, who may or may not pay us back in ten years or 15 years or what have you. Not only are we loaning those jurisdictions billions of dollars, but we are doing so at very advantageous rates compared to the prevalent interest rates in this country.
When considering the bill before us we should reflect on how we arrived at the point where we are being asked tonight to give one Crown corporation the right to bind the Queen in the name of Canada to the extent of $26 billion. In this connection I would point out that the Export Development Corporation, as most members realize, was established by an act of parliament on October 1, 1969. It replaced at that time the 25-year old Export Credits Insurance Corporation. The original act underwent major revisions in 1974. There were minor revisions in 1971, 1973 and 1977.
Bill C-36 incorporates a $26 billion package, as I have stated. That is a package of $26 billion compared to the present loan authorizations, insurance and guarantee obligations within the Crown corporations, EDC, at this time of $8.85 billion. Now we are faced with this revision.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to put on the record the plateaux which we have hit in the evolution of the Export Development Corporation. First of all dealing with the authorized capital in the act, this is found in subsection (11). Initially the authorized capital in this corporation was set at $25 million. That was in 1969, just a year after the emperor took power in Canada. In 1971 authorized capital was raised to $75 million. In 1973 it was raised to $125 million. In 1974 it went up to $400 million. It is proposed in Bill C-36 that the authorized capital should be a mere $1 billion compared to a capital in this corporation of $25 million in 1969.
Let us look at the corporate insurance activities which are set out in section 26 of the Export Development Act. There we find that in 1969 the initial authorization that this parliament gave this corporation was $250 million. By 1971 it was raised
April 24, 1978

to $500 million, by 1974 $750 million and by 1977 $2,500 million. Bill C-36 before us now proposes that that corporation's insurance authorization will be $10 billion compared to the $250 million authorization in 1969.
That is the corporate side of insurance with regard to EDC. On the government side, which is another department that this corporation administers, we find that the total government authorization in 1969 was $500 million. In 1974 it was raised to $750 million and, by 1977, it was an even $1 billion. Tonight it is being proposed in Bill C-36 that that particular section should go up to $3,500 million, or $3!/2 billion. That is being asked for in the bill before us. Compare that to a total insurance authorization on the government side under section 28 of this act of $500 million in 1969.
Let us look at how they have escalated their authorization for loan activity. It is the loan activity in which Canada is most vulnerable. We find under section 30 of the original act the total authorization for this corporation was $600 million. That was in 1969. In 1971 they raised it to $850 million and in 1973 to $1,500 million. In 1974, hon. members will recall, it was raised to $414 billion. I am now talking about the authorization for Export Development Corporation to lend to foreign governments and foreign entities. In Bill C-36, they are now asking for an authorization of $10 billion compared to $600 million in 1969.
The act is divided into two sides. On the corporate side there is $10 billion for foreign governments and other entities. On the government side, they are asking for an authorization of $2'/2 billion. That compares to an authorization for this corporation in 1969 of $200 million. In 1971 it was $450 million and in 1974 it was $850 million.
As can be seen from the foregoing, the growth of EDC has been sporadic but it has been significant. Perhaps I can show it best if I bring together the various levels of authorization that they are now seeking. The total value of 1969 EDC authorizations was $1,550 million, in short a little higher than $114 billion. If the bill goes through tonight, the total value of authorizations awarded to EDC will be $26 billion. This is why I caution hon. members initially to view this bill with a great deal of scrutiny. When we are talking in terms of EDC having the authority as a corporation to loan $10 billion, let us not forget that a good portion of that $10 billion may never be repaid and will have to be written off.
As we know, certain write-offs, or reschedulings as they are called, have already been taking place in EDC with respect to some of the lending activity they have entered into. In this connection, I refer hon. members to the Auditor General's report with respect to the Export Development Corporation for the year ended December 31, 1977.
In that report, the Auditor General points out that under the Export Development Act the corporation, meaning EDC, may have outstanding loans to foreign borrowers, outstanding guarantee agreements to other lenders and signed but undisbursed loan and guarantee agreements up to a maximum of $4,250 million at any time. That is where we now sit if Bill C-36 does not go through.
Export Development Act
He then points out that as at December 31, 1977 the position of the corporation is as follows: Loans receivable, $1,833 million, less certain participations which he lists of $40 million, for a net outstanding loans receivable position with respect to the corporation, EDC, of $1,793 million. The Auditor General then points out that there are guarantees for which the corporation is contingently liable of $8,479,000 and undisbursed funds under signed loan agreements of $1,647 million. All of those total-and I know you are very fast in arithmetic, Mr. Speaker-$3,449 million.
In short, you can see where the panic is. They have already committed or disbursed almost $314 billion of their total authorization of $414 billion. They had done that as of December 31. Now they rush into this House with the bill before us and say the sky is falling, pass it quickly or our authorization is going to be exceeded.
If that is true, there can be no more basic fundamental criticism of this government than that they have handled their affairs in a leisurely, unconcerned fashion. They have allowed a Crown corporation to run up obligations bringing it within its total authorization limit. Second, knowing that this is occurring, they did not bring this bill in in proper time to ensure there could be ample debate in the House, without suggesting that somehow we have to be stampeded into an early passage of the bill.
I wanted to give the House that background as to why the urgency tonight. The fact is limits previously set by parliament are now coming into view as far as EDC is concerned and there is a bit of panic on the government side.
The other point I would like to emphasize is that the Auditor General points out that they are up to their old hanky panky. They are rescheduling loans. This is the classic way that loan corporations cover bad bills of yesteryear. Here is what the Auditor General says:
During 1977, the Corporation rescheduled payments due of $3,942,000. These reschedulings are intended to aid collectibility and servicing of the debt. Since inception of the export loans program in 196i, the corporation has rescheduled $65,377,000, of which $591,000 is overdue at December 31, 1977.
If you have any trouble in the lending business, you never admit it. You never like to talk about write-offs. That means the mistake is very obvious. What you do is bring in the person to whom you are creditor. You tell him he would feel better and you would feel better if you both sat down, wrote a new note for the principal, the interest and a new fresh date and he would go away and have a happy Christmas and you would have an even happier Christmas. Mr. Speaker, they are at it already. Yet they have the colossal nerve to come to this House and say: Quick, give us further authorization which will allow us to put out another $10 billion, because our limit is now in sight with respect to total disbursements.
What the Auditor General has said was also revealed in the documentation which the Export Development Corporation has been filing in Washington in accordance with the United States security and exchange regulations. In this connection

April 24, 1978
Export Development Act
we recall that we presently have a government which, when it was faced with borrowing abroad to cover the current account deficit and other things, had to file a presentation revealing, for the first time in the past decade certainly, exactly what was the state of affairs in Canada. They did that in March. They had to rush the presentation through so as to be in a position to include figures only up to March 31, 1978, because they realized that if they filed in April or later they would have to show not just the 1978 figures but the 1979 figures also. They had to come clean, because they realized they had to make a clean breast of it to the securities and exchange commission in the United States. So did the Export Development Corporation.
I would invite every member of the House before voting on this bill to take a look at some of the dealings which have been going on. I have a document here called a confidential private placement offering memorandum. In this presentation the corporation is selling notes due in exchange for $50 million U.S. The presentation is dated June, 1977. I draw this to your attention, Mr. Speaker, because here again the corporation has been obliged to reveal some of the rescheduling which has been going on. On page 62 of the presentation it is stated:
Since the inception of the program, loan payments totalling $61.2 million have been rescheduled, of which $15.9 million had been repaid by December 31, 1976. Interest rates on rescheduled loans have been generally at the same or higher rates. On other loans, principal instalments totalling $1.8 million were overdue at December 31, 1976. No loans have been written off since inception of the international lending program, but one loan was cancelled at no loss to EDC under an arrangment with the Government of Canada to cancel a corresponding amount due from EDC.
The crunch comes with the last line. The EDC likes to represent itself as never having to write off a loan. It acknowledges that loans have been rescheduled, but that is all. However, in the filing they had to make in Washington the corporation admits that one loan was cancelled, though at no loss to the EDC. Do you know what they are up to there, Mr. Speaker? They got into trouble with a country. The Government of Canada stepped in and went to the assistance of the debtor by lending that country money so that it could in turn pay back the EDC and clear the loan. But guess who pays the shot in the final analysis? It is the Canadian taxpayer. That is the result of the comfortable relationship which exists between this corporation and the government of the day.
One of the most serious things that is occurring with regard to federal government spending is the tendency of Treasury Board and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to misrepresent the spending figures of Canada. It is traditional when dealing with budgetary matters to include all spending, to include whatever our Crown corporations are spending in addition to normal budgetary expenditures. However, if hon. members look at the budget brought in on April 10 they will find there is a little footnote which states that the expenditures of the Government of Canada do not include certain Crown corporation activities. Under government policy, it is stated, such activities will no longer be included in the over-all picture.
[Mr. Stevens.)
When we press to find out why EDC borrowing is not automatically included as part of the government's financial picture, we are told that these arrangements are not binding upon the Government of Canada, that somehow or other EDC is raising the money on its own signature and that the Government of Canada does not have the eventual obligation to pay a debt in the event of a default. Mr. Speaker, if we look at the filing in Washington to which I have referred, we find this is not true. At page 12 of the document asking the Americans to lend the EDC money the following statement appears:
The notes will be direct unsecured general obligations of EDC and as such will constitute an obligation of Her Majesty in right of Canada. Payment of principal and interest on the notes will be a charge on and payable out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada. Issuance of the notes is subject to the approval of the Minister of Finance of Canada and the notes will be created pursuant to resolution of the EDC board of directors.
In short, the notes are being sold in the United States as direct obligations of the Crown without any equivocation. I think it is altogether misleading for cabinet ministers to be stating they are not obligations of the Crown in the right of Canada and that they need not, therefore, be included in this country's expenditure figures.
When it was instituted in 1969, Mr. Speaker, the EDC was a comparatively small corporation. The government is now proposing that it blossom into a $26 billion organization, making it one of the largest export development corporations in the world. I would suggest the corporation is engaging in leading activity which, in all likelihood, will result in a severe loss factor to be reckoned with in future years. Further, I would suggest that, contrary to what has been said, the obligations it is incurring, as the expression goes, offshore in the American or Eurodollar market are obligations of the Government of Canada and not, as ministers are representing, simply obligations of this Crown corporation.
A number of my hon. friends have dealt with certain of the lending activities in which this corporation has been engaged. If I may, I should like to mention some of the highlights of this activity. It goes without saying it is nice to feel one is supporting exports if those exports create jobs for Canadians. Who could disagree with that proposition? But we should bear in mind that there are two ways of looking at this. There is the short term perspective, the immediate creation of jobs. But in the longer term is it in the interest of Canada to be creating competition for our own businessmen in future years? It is this side of the corporation's activity which the government is ignoring.
The competition this agency is helping to foster in the pulp and paper industry is something about which the government should concern itself. Was it, for example, proper to announce, as the corporation did on February 8, 1974, that it was putting $82.5 million into an integrated forestry complex in Iran, a country which hardly knows what to do with its United States dollar surpluses? Here we were pumping $82.5 million into that country to help it with its forestry development, and later we were begging in Washington for $750 million to help us withstand the fall in our dollar resulting from our current account deficit.
April 24, 1978

That is not the only loan the corporation has made in the forestry field. On October 17, 1976 the corporation put out $102 million to help a pulp and paper mill in Poland, of all places. I will come back to that in a minute. On September 21, 1977 the corporation put out $1.8 million for a pulp and paper mill project in Peru. On November 8, 1977, joining, as the corporation sometimes does, with one of our chartered banks-this time it was the Bank of Montreal-the corporation put out $102.6 million for a new pulp and paper mill in Iran. Iran again. The government tells us in the Toronto area that it does not have a nickel to mitigate the urban transportation plight of people going to and from work in Toronto. The EDC has $102.6 million for Iran, but according to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) the government has no money for urban transportation in Toronto.
That very same government told the fishermen on our east and west coasts that it has no money to help them refurbish their fishing fleets so that they can fish the allotments off both coasts which should be theirs. That very same government cannot help the city of Montreal with its sewage treatment problems. Montreal is a large city which has no sewage treatment facilities to speak of. The government says it has no money for that, but it has, as I have said, hundreds of millions of dollars to help other countries build pulp and paper and forestry plants which in coming years will end up competing with our own pulp and paper industry.
Let me give other examples. On December 28, 1977, between Christmas and New Year's Day, the corporation put up $5.5 million for a pulp and paper project in Romania. On March 8, 1978, again with bank participation, the corporation announced loans totalling $57 million for two pulp and paper projects in Argentina. I notice, Mr. Speaker, that you are fast with your pencil. If Your Honour has been following what I have been saying, Your Honour will know that the corporation has put up something like $350 million to help others build pulp and paper and forestry developments which will compete with us, yet the government tells us there is no money to help with some of the infrastructure needs which exist in Canada.
There is no money, for example, to help with the building of the Bay of Fundy power project. There is no money to help with the electrical project in Labrador. There is no money to help the farmers of western Canada with their grain handling problems. Where has the perspective gone? Why is there money for these types of foreign activities which are risky but which, granted, give us perhaps one year's employment, but no money for the infrastructures and services which are needed so urgently in Canada and which could also provide employment in Canada?
I will go on. On October 24, 1977, $78 million was the total amount of loans for nickel mining projects in Guatemala and Indonesia. On December 28, 1977, $2.95 million was put up for the production of steel products in Los Angeles, California. 1 was down there just a few months ago, and that is a boom area. Here we were, again just after Christmas-Christmas must make the corporation open up in a very expansive way-
Export Development Act
putting up $2.95 million to help with the production of steel products in Los Angeles, California.
Where are they going to get this money?

My colleague from Nova Scotia asks where they will get this money. We know where. The money will come from private markets, both domestic and international. The corporation will raise the money as best it can, but above all it will be binding the people of Canada to those obligations. Our point is that if money like that is capable of being raised, certainly a portion of it could be diverted to help Canadians and to meet Canadian needs. Frankly, some of the countries into which we are pouring money are in much better shape than we are internationally, so it is time this government regained some sanity.
On January 18, 1978 the EDC put $3.6 million into a company in Colorado to help it buy Dash-7 aircraft. The governmet is at all ends of these deals. It owns DeHavilland. There are loans amounting to something over $100 million to keep DeHavilland going, and now the government is at the other end lending money to the buyers of Dash-7 aircraft. On January 27, 1978 the EDC put up $30.6 million for the construction of an aluminum plant in Ireland.
I think it has already been mentioned that on February 13, 1978 the corporation lent $47 million for a ministeel mill in New Jersey. That loan meant that the government had put up $100 million for steel mills in Texas, Minnesota, Great Britain and in New Jersey. The steel people of this country say that there is no doubt that they will have to meet that competition whenever it comes on stream with its new facilities.
I have already referred to certain communist countries which have been picking up these loans. The EDC has advanced financing to the following communist countries: Russia, Poland, Yugoslavia, Cuba, Czechoslovakia, Romania, Hungary and Bulgaria. In that respect I think there are two important things to bear in mind. If we finance facilities in Cuba, Poland or some other such country, we are dealing with an entirely different environment from that which exists in Canada. A state planned economy can impose virtually any wage structure it wishes for its export development activities. Here we are helping communist countries build facilities which will compete with ours. We are ignoring the fact that they can compete with us with wage structures of their own choosing. Second, we are making loans to countries such as Cuba, which sees fit to have armed troops in other countries basically for revolutionary purposes.
This government has a strange double standard. It sees nothing wrong with that. But let the shoe be on the other foot and the government is quick to give lip service to any revolutionary group which may be acting in some country which is not of communist persuasion. These are the hard facts, and when the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce comes before us and says "Quick, let's pass this bill", I say he just has not read the bill or does not understand what the EDC is doing. How can he seriously expect members of this House to jump into line and allow early passage of this bill?
4818

April 24, 1978
Export Development Act
I have referred to communist countries which have been picking up our credit. I could run over the list, but in total they have picked up about $375 million in loans. There are extensive lines of credit out in addition to that amount. Loans to Arab bloc and oil-rich nations total a further $275.8 million. The point is that if funds amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars are available, surely the government, if it should so will, could be finding at least a portion of those funds for urgently needed Canadian developments such as the ones I have itemized.
My colleague the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) touched on what I think is one of the most serious developments that has occurred in any Crown corporation, that is that a Crown corporation, I take it with the consent if not the specific direction of its president, has chosen to openly criticize members of the House who choose to speak about what they feel are irresponsible EDC activities. My colleague the hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton (Mr. Scott) has dealt quite well with this. He has rebutted the statement put out by EDC in his report from parliament dated January 26, 1978.
Frankly, I think it is unfortunate that any member of the House has to deal with a Crown corporation in that way. Surely if EDC, or any other Crown corporation, feels that a member of the House has raised some facts that should be challenged, the proper way to challenge them is through the responsible minister in the House or at a committee meeting. They should not feel that they have the right to go even to the ridings of members of parliament and attempt to blackmail them-because that is what it is-into being less vocal in their criticism of their activities. When you think of it, Mr. Speaker, where are we going to end up in this country if the 380 odd Crown corporations which exist all decide that they, using public funds, have the right regularly to criticize the activities of members in the House who, after all, are supposed to be elected to supervise the very activities of those Crown corporations?
Hear, hear!

This is the dangerous precedent that has been set by this corporation. Before this bill is passed, I think we need some clarification, not just from the minister but from the executive of EDC. Do they intend to pursue this type of harassment in future months and years? Do they feel that they no longer have to answer to the Parliament of Canada through the relevant minister but that they have the prerogative to openly challenge members of parliament in whatever statements they care to make concerning that corporation's activities?
I notice representatives of EDC sitting in the gallery. They laugh when I make these points. This is no laughing affair. I think it is high time that EDC was called to task for this kind of conduct.
There are some more serious matters that I would like to touch upon, but I notice my time is starting to run out. Let me say that here we have a bill which must be given in depth study before it is passed. In no way should the Parliament of Canada be expected to rubber stamp this type of legislation without intensive review, not only during debate but in committee when the bill reaches that stage.
I know that one or two of my colleagues wish to participate in this debate, so perhaps I will give them an opportunity, although time is running out. I will have more to say on this important bill at report stage, in committee and at third reading. But let there be no doubt that we in the opposition feel there are significant comments to be made about this corporation and this legislation, and the government had better not look to us for any rubber stamping.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Young (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are only a few minutes left this evening before time runs out and I think I can make my remarks in those few minutes.
I know from past history that the hon. member who has just spoken has visited the area I represent, and I also know that the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) who sits just behind him will be visiting that area tomorrow night. I only hope they will go down there and make those kinds of comments in my area again because that will assure not only me but the Liberal candidate in that riding a sound election victory. I would love to have them go down and make those kinds of comments because I think it is about time somebody said a few good words about EDC.
I would like to tell the hon. member, who is so afraid of these EDC helpful purchases, contracts and guarantees of purchases which involve countries that do not share our political philosophy but follow the communist one, that today in the riding of Niagara Falls there are some 150 men back at work who did not have a job two years ago. They work in a brand new plant which was opened just last year because EDC had enough good business sense to back a company in that riding which wanted to sell some trucks to the Soviet Union. That company in my riding, called Unit Rig, which makes giant earth moving equipment, has now, with the successful completion of a couple of bargaining contracts with EDC, managed to undertake sales contracts for some 50 trucks for some $85 million worth of business, and thanks to EDC there are some 100 men working in that plant. I think that EDC deserves laudatory credit for that.
If that is not enough, I would like to point out one other instance. In the same riding last year there was a great deal of unemployment as a result of a number of factors which came together at one time. Another firm by the name of Horton Steel had all its contracts in one basket with the Ontario government through Hydro to make pressure vessels and steel fabricating necessities for nuclear power projects. When the Ontario government cancelled those contracts it had to shut down the plant. That meant that 200 men were laid off for three to four months straight through. But because of EDC, because of some intervention and because of an aggressive

April 24, 1978

sales force on the part of Horton Steel, they were able to get a contract to build in Indonesia part of a cement factory built by Catinho Caro. They had some work involving a $22 million contract and they put 200 men in the community of Fort Erie to work, men who did not have jobs.
I hope that hon. members on the other side will come to my riding. I invite them to go there and criticize EDC and some of the job creation projects that we in the Liberal government have undertaken in the last year, because the people there will not buy that kind of nonsense. It is about time that the hon. member who has just spoken investigated some of the facts and gave a little credit to EDC.
With that I will conclude my comments, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: HEALTH-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF BAN ON SACCHARIN
HEALTH-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF BAN ON SACCHARIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 17, after the Appeal Court of Quebec confirmed what we all suspected-that the sugar companies were a monopoly victimizing the consumer by price fixing-I asked the question which surely must have been on everyone's mind that day about the announcement by the former minister of national health and welfare that saccharin will be banned. He claimed that some rats, creatures prone to cancer, showed signs of bladder cancer in what he declared were scientific experiments.
The Quebec decision was handed down, and I asked the present minister for an independent investigation to be made from outside her department to review the research on saccharin. Tonight I would like to ask her to go further and seek an independent investigation of the strange coincidence of the monopoly being cleared in the courts, and then so soon after that the saccharin ban being announced in the House.
Remarkably, no one in the department told the House that these rats were in fact cancer prone, or that they were given excessive quantities of saccharin to prove that three out of one hundred would get cancer, or might get cancer, as a matter of fact. That was the equivalent, if given to humans of comparable weight, of 20,000 grains or 40,000 teaspoons of sugar as
Adjournment Debate
a sweetener, or 800 cans of pop or the equivalent of drinking a bathtub of diet pop a day.
The federal drug administration in the United States found no evidence that saccharin had caused cancer in humans during the 80 years it has been used by diabetics and, latterly, by overweight people.
Experiments with Rhesus monkeys by Dr. Frederick Coul-ston of Albany, New York, showed saccharin was not dangerous. Dr. Coulston gave the monkeys moderately high doses of saccharin for seven years, and not one contracted cancer. I would like to think humans are more like monkeys than rats, but sometimes, of course, we have a few qualms and doubts about that. The longer one stays in the House, the greater the doubt.
In fact, the International Toxicology Forum in Omaha, U.S.A., in May of 1977 had already come to the conclusion that the frequency of bladder cancer in the Canadian rat experiments was probably not primarily due to saccharin but could be attributed to other circumstances, such as increased formation of micro-stones in the bladder or increased stress. Professor C. H. Slatter, Director of the Institute of Toxicology at the University of Zurich, was able to prove that the artificial sweetener "possesses none of the typical characteristics of chemical carcinogens".
Professor Dieter Schmahl of the German Cancer Research Centre in Heidelberg, after two years of saccharin experiments with pregnant rats, has only this to say so far:
-the fact that it was even possible to apply a food additive in such large overdoses as in the Canadian experiment for a whole lifetime, attest mainly that it is not poisonous.
The British Medical Journal, The Lancet, reinforced this by citing the study by the Americans Wynder and Goldsmith, which concluded that "users of saccharin have a smaller risk of bladder cancer than non users".
It is remarkable that the Canadian scientists, with the huge laboratory of Canadian people who have had saccharin for almost 90 years for the care and control of diabetes, and for overweight, had to go to the rats for this ludicrous experiment in order to get this valuable and vital substance banned.
One has to look at the timing of the ban in Canada. It was for this reason I asked my question. I did not get a satisfactory answer. The sugar companies raised their prices excessively, no doubt a greed impulse which they knew they could carry off because they were a monopoly. The price went up, as I recall, from about 30 cents a pound to about a dollar. Many Canadian consumers found alternatives, knowing that sugar, especially refined sugar, is dangerous to health. They either reduced or cut out the use of sugar altogether, or learned to use saccharin or honey as substitutes.
The then minister of consumer and corporate affairs, the present Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), charged that sugar group under the combines act. He lost that first round. The whole country trusted and believed he was right. As you recall, he also believed he was right and he stuck to that. This caused him considerable trouble, and nobody

Shortly after, the ban was announced in this House of Commons. There was no debate in this House as to whether it should be banned or not.
