speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH-REQUEST FOR REVIEW OF BAN ON SACCHARIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) for putting forth a very strong argument, as she always does; and she did it very effectively on March 17 when she asked another question of the minister of health and welfare. The whole question, of course, is one of risk-benefit, the risk to the individual who uses saccharin and/or the benefit that may be derived if you happen to be a diabetic or somebody who needs this kind of sweetener. The health protection branch of the department of health and welfare has deemed it necessary and in the interests of Canadians to ban saccharin. This has been carried out and recommended by the World Health Organization as well. I would point out to the hon. member that Canada is not the only country that has banned saccharin, Holland has done likewise.
With regard to questions that have been raised concerning the scientific validity of the Canadian tests on saccharin and the need for independent scientific review of the data the following points should be noted.
The Canadian saccharin test was designed and conducted according to internationally acceptable guidelines for the assessment of the potential carcinogenicity of food ingredients. These guidelines have been enunciated by the World Health Organization and the U.S. National Cancer Institute and are in use worldwide.
When the Canadian tests were completed in March 1977, an independent board of world renowned pathologists was assembled to review the lesions noted in the animals fed saccharin. This board of pathologists arrived at a consensus diagnosis regarding the bladder tumors in the animals and this consensus has been universally accepted by scientists worldwide.
The results of the Canadian tests have been presented to the World Health Organization, and to several independent scientific organizations including the Society of Toxicology and the Toxicology Forum. These groups have endorsed the contention that saccharin is unequivocally carcinogenic in animals and a potential carcinogen for humans. In fact, at the 1977 Joint Expert Committee Meeting on Food Additives held under the auspices of the World Health Organization in Geneva it was recommended that severe limitations be placed on the use of saccharin in food products.
The commissioner, U.S. food and drug administration, after reviewing all data on saccharin and particularly the results of the Canadian tests, concluded that saccharin must be considered a potential carcinogen for humans. Intent to establish regulations prohibiting the sale of saccharin in food products was published by the commission in the Federal Register of April 15, 1977.
At the request of Senator Edward M. Kennedy's sub-committee on health and scientific research, the office of technology assessment was asked to assemble a distinguished panel of scientists to summarize all the known facts regarding the carcinogenic effects of saccharin. The OTA is an arm of Congress set up to provide Congress with an independent appraisal of complex scientific matters.
The following are conclusions of the OTA that related to the cancer producing potential of saccharin. First, laboratory evidence indicates that saccharin is a carcinogen. Second, prolonged ingestion of saccharin at high levels caused a significant increase in the incidence of bladder cancer in rats in three independent experiments. Earlier tests, which were negative, were not sensitive enough to detect this carcinogenic effect. Third, this evidence leads to the conclusion that saccharin is a potential cause of cancer in humans.
A further discussion of the OTA's report and additional information concerning the validity of the Canadian tests has been published in Hansard, Tuesday, June 14, 1977.
[Mrs. Holt.)
April 24, 1978

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-NORTHERN ONTARIO-CALL FOR INQUIRY INTO AIR SAFETY
AIR TRANSPORT-NORTHERN ONTARIO-CALL FOR INQUIRY INTO AIR SAFETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 20 I requested that an inquiry be conducted into air safety in northern Ontario in light of the evidence presented by the Association of Treaty Chiefs located in Timmins, Ontario, who have compiled a rather lengthy document on air transportation problems in northern Ontario, particularly air safety.
In part of the minister's answer to me he stated that I used a lot of outdated information. Mr. Speaker, I have concerned myself with air safety problems since 1973. The information I have been using has been supplied to me from employees in the Department of Transport on a continuing basis since then. Much of the information was a couple of years old-not outdated but no action had been taken by senior officials in the Department of Transport. These employees come to me on a continuing basis because they are so concerned about the senior officials in the Department of Transport not acting on air safety regulations in Canada.
In his answer on April 20 the minister stated:
... the smaller carriers in this country adopt very high standards indeed, and I would not like to see them smeared in this way.
The minister was referring to me. At no time was I smearing the small carriers.
I should like to quote from an article in a recent issue of the Canadian Flight magazine. The article was written by the small carriers. It begins:
... We should all be very wary of the background of those in high office who make decisions that affect general aviation operations.
Later the article goes on:
Walt McLeish is a case in point. As top man-administrator of DOT'S Canadian Air Transportation Administration-Walt feels that his background as a professional aeronautical engineer (Masters Degree from Michigan State; RCAF trained pilot) qualifies him to speak authoritatively on general aviation.
The industry isn't inclined to give him that respect, deserving though it may be. In spite of his excellent reputation as a good government administrator,...
I will provide this whole document to the parliamentary secretary tonight. They do not have faith in Mr. McLeish.
Tonight, Mr. Speaker, I have been informed that there are no visual approach indicating systems at 60 airports in Canada. I will check that out further. In his answer the minister commented that my references were to matters that happened in the nineteenth century. Mr. Speaker, it was not the nineteenth century but March 9, 1978 when I raised the subject before.
The document from the treaty Indians is rather lengthy and it contains some startling statements. It opens with a quote from a witness to the Hartt Commission in Ontario as follows:
There is an appalling lack of proper air navigational aids, weather facilities, and all weather day and night airports ... The mode of operation has in the large part, changed very little since the 1930's ... The further north you go, the more the bush flying ethic prevails.
This refers to air safety in northern Ontario. The report goes on to say:
Adjournment Debate
This report should be considered as an introduction to the study of air transportation in northern Ontario. For many people who live in the north, it is a fact that air transportation is hazardous. Many of us have encountered horrendous experiences, ranging from non-fatal crashes, to running out of gas upon landing. Just recently, the vice president of the central region of Grand Council Treaty #9 was stranded in the bush after the plane in which he was a passenger crashed to the ground. Luckily there were no injuries. He witnessed the fact that this aircraft contained no medical equipment, food, rifles, or sleeping bags for emergency situations. This situation is only one of the many that we hear about when living in the north.
You can see my concern, Mr. Speaker, and the concern of the treaty Indians who prepared a statement of this length. I am not interested in continuing to hear these smart aleck answers of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) regarding matters as serious as this. The report continues:
In this report I do not choose to point a finger at the companies who are responsible for air transportation. However, I do wish to examine the situation as it has been reported to me, and experienced by me, and I also choose to discuss the struggle we have had in trying to convince the government of the need for a transportation inquiry.
I can certainly sympathize with them there, Mr. Speaker. We have been calling for this public inquiry for the last year and a half. I received recently a document dated February 25, 1977 from employees of the Department of Transport. I am informed the information is relevant today and that no action is being taken on this very serious study done on weather irregularities, reports and landing regulations. Among other things this document, which is a Government of Canada document, says this:
Pilots have chosen to ignore limits for various reasons, not the least of which may have been pressure from management, but mainly because of the unenforceability of present regulations. Also the present inaccuracies in measurement of ceiling and visibility in the take-off or touchdown zone have led pilots to come and go at will. The only time action is taken to curb this dangerous practice is when accidents occur.
It goes on to say:
There are several recent known instances which very nearly resulted in serious accidents in this Region-
The region referred to is the Atlantic region.
-all partially attributable to landings completed when the reported weather was below limits. In none of these cases was enforcement action taken by this Ministry mainly because the Official Weather Report is not accepted as proof of existing weather conditions.
It continues:
While the following recommendations may seem drastic and past fatality records in Canada where weather has been proven to be a factor may not appear to bear out their use, unless action is taken to improve the existing situation the probability exists that a major accident will occur soon.
I hope the Ministry of Transport will not wait until there is a major accident before taking some decisive action. There was a serious accident recently at Cranbrook. All the people to whom I have spoken point out that it is the senior executives in the Ministry of Transport who are the ones not enforcing these regulations. It is disturbing that these conditions exist in this country and absolutely nothing is being done about them. These people telephone me and come to my office with this documented evidence. I and other members have brought this

April 24, 1978
Adjournment Debate
matter repeatedly before the House of Commons but nothing is being done by this minister that we are aware of.
It is stated that runways should be closed when bad weather conditions zero in. But this is not done. It is all by chance and by golly.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-NORTHERN ONTARIO-CALL FOR INQUIRY INTO AIR SAFETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can only begin my remarks by deploring the comments made by the hon. member concerning an official of the Department of Transport whose energy and outstanding competence are devoted to make Canadian civil aviation one of the best and safest in the world. Furthermore, I think that the competence of that official has never been contested and that his reputation is recognized not only in Canada but also in the aviation circles in foreign countries.
First as concerns the report on air transportation in northern Ontario, dated March 21, 1978, it is being reviewed by departmental officials. But at first glance the report which includes quotations from the Hartt Commission report, the report on the study of air safety in northern Ontario prepared by department inspectors, and articles from newspapers and other documents does not seem to include any new information or facts that would give to the government any reason to believe that an inquiry commission on air transportation in northern Ontario should be established.
Since January 1978, regional inspectors of Transport Canada have made many inspections of air carriers in this area. Those inspections have identified minor infractions in the operations of those carriers but nothing important has been unveiled to justify the temporary withdrawal of an operation license or other sanctions. The government intends to ensure strict surveillance of air carriers in this area, particularly those that have been identified by the inquiry on air safety in northern Ontario.

As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has stated in the House on several occasions, he is confident that the various measures which are in the process of implementation, for example, additional manpower resources to permit increased surveillance of air carrier operations, will adequately reinforce the licensing and inspection systems of air carriers not only in northern Ontario but throughout Canada.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I should like to caution the hon. member opposite not to create false impressions about aviation safety in Canada. Canada has one of the finest safety records in the world, because most air carriers are responsible and respectable and meet, and usually surpass, high regulation requirements.

subtopic: MANPOWER-JOB VACANCIES BEING FILLED BY PERSONS OUTSIDE PROVINCE
MANPOWER-JOB VACANCIES BEING FILLED BY PERSONS OUTSIDE PROVINCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions I have raised in the House concerns about northern Manitoba where the student unemployment rate is one of the highest in Canada. On March 22, page 4016 of Hansard, I put forth a motion under Standing Order 43. It did not carry and therefore could not be debated.
On April 4,1 directed a question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), page 4112 of Hansard, asking what was being done about the financing of transportation of students from Shawinigan, Quebec to Flin Flon, Manitoba. In 1976, 25 students from Shawinigan received preferential treatment in receiving student jobs in Flin Flon, Manitoba. Presumably because of a corporate policy, the Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting Company hired a certain number of French students during the summer. I do not know if it was because Shawinigan is in the constituency of the Minister of Finance, (Mr. Chretien), but these 25 students received transportation grants from Canada Manpower.
I have been told by officials in Winnipeg and in Flin Flon that there is no program to cover transportation costs from their homes to jobs unless there is a reciprocal agreement. This was not a reciprocal agreement. Therefore, these students received preferential treatment in filling those jobs.
I brought this to the minister's attention through the media because I was not receiving any replies to the letters I had written. In a story printed in the Ottawa Journal and the Winnipeg Free Press I expressed my feelings about students in the north not getting a fair shake with regard to those jobs.
After my motion under Standing Order 43 and my questions to the Minister of Employment and Immigration, I received a letter from the minister. I feel that unemployed students in Flin Flon, Shawinigan or any other part of the country should all receive the same treatment. However, those from Shawinigan received preferential treatment. They received air tickets from Shawinigan to Flin Flon, with no obligation to stay on the job or to repay the money. As I said, there was no program that this situation fitted into.
The staff in the Winnipeg regional office were infuriated over this order that came from on high. I think there was a deal between the Minister of Finance and someone in Manpower to pay the transportation costs of these students. The counsellors in the Flin Flon Manpower office had students to place into those jobs, but they were bypassed. The office in Flin Flon was in the position where they had been dealing with the employer and the students. They then found these jobs were being filled with students receiving preferential treatment.
It took two years to get this clarified in a letter from the minister. In 1977, there were supposed to be 25 students going to Flin Flon. However, because of the concern I felt that the students in Flin Flon were not getting the same treatment, only eight went from Shawinigan to Flin Flon. The minister says, in his letter:
April 24, 1978

In the past years, the commission has assisted this movement through small mobility grants, because of the then much lower student unemployment levels in Flin Flon than in Shawinigan.
The general rise in unemployment levels has, however, changed the situation expected this summer and we do not, accordingly, feel that repetition of such assistance would be justified during the summer of 1978.
The basic situation for this summer thus appears to be that the company is likely to continue its past policy of providing summer jobs in Flin Flon to a number of students from Quebec, but that the commission will not be providing any financial assistance in respect of the movement.
That is really what I was after. As I said earlier, I felt that students from Shawinigan or in other communities competing for the jobs in the mining communities in the north where opportunities are limited should get the same treatment as others, not preferential treatment in circumstances where the minister-because Shawinigan is in his constituency-put pressure on Manpower to pay transportation costs.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MANPOWER-JOB VACANCIES BEING FILLED BY PERSONS OUTSIDE PROVINCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member will share with me the positive side of that experience, namely that students from Shawinigan should go to Flin Flon, and I dare hope that one day, Mr. Speaker, students from Flin Flon will go to Shawinigan, or Tadoussac or Matane and that students from Matane and all those towns and cities in Quebec will go somewhere in Manitoba and other Canadian provinces because it is on that basis of student exchanges that we can build a better Canada.
However, Mr. Speaker, the implication that the Minister of Finance was in any way involved in the decision of the manpower centre or the manpower commission to pay for the transportation of those students from Shawinigan to Flin Flon seems to me to be quite regrettable. I think it also denotes very poor knowledge of the operation of Canada manpower centres to dare even imagine that the Minister of Finance or anyone else in this House could influence any manpower centre in the application of their program.
I would like to continue my remarks by mentioning that it has been the policy of the Hudson's Bay Mining and Smelting Company since 1976 to hire a small number of French-speaking students from Shawinigan, Quebec, for the summer at its
Adjournment Debate
operations in Flin Flon, Manitoba. I am informed that the company has decided to continue that policy in 1978. The hon. member will appreciate that this is a policy decided entirely by that company-our Canada employment centres fill the job applications they receive but cannot control the policy of the company in this area.
In past years the commission helped students get to the work site of the Hudson's Bay Mining and Smelting Company in Flin Flon through small mobility subsidies covering travel expenses and a small per diem of $20 per student for their housing needs. Mobility grants of this kind are generally available to students only if there is a shortage of qualified workers in the community where they are going to work. In past years, there was a low rate of unemployment around Flin Flon, whereas in Shawinigan the rate of unemployment among students was rather high, which enabled the commission to have a relatively broad policy in the area, particularly from the point of view of the benefits stemming from such cultural exchanges.
Unfortunately it will not be possible for the commission to approve mobility assistance grants for the 10 or 15 Quebec students seeking jobs in Flin Flon this year. The employment situation for students in Flin Flon is not as favourable as in the past. So it will be impossible to meet the request of the Quebec students and consider once again this modest form of financial assistance.

It appears that regardless of the commission's policy with respect to student mobility grants, Hudson's Bay Mining and Smelting is likely to continue its practice of providing a small number of summer jobs to students from Quebec. As I mentioned earlier, this is not a matter in which the employment and immigration commission can properly intervene since the selection of employees is a matter of private sector decision making. The commission is not in any way assisting this movement; neither is it hindering it nor is it in a position to hinder it.
